problem:
Research Orchid (orchid.ai), formerly Zero and Mail0, from public pages only.

The client problem: an email product wants an agent to take a thread. Decide how Orchid should hand a thread to an agent without dropping the conversation, and which artifacts the team needs.

Do not claim the company commissioned this work. Use only public sources.

market.summary: Orchid (orchid.ai), formerly Zero/Mail0, is publicly positioned as an approval-first personal assistant that runs inbox triage, calendar, meeting prep, travel, and follow-ups, living in Gmail, Google Calendar, and SMS with drafts staying drafts until approved (orchid.ai/llms.txt). The public FAQ says it quietly handles email, calendar, meeting prep, and travel (orchid.ai/faq), and the homepage frames it as an assistant reached through messages that connects to the user's stack (orchid.ai/). The legacy Zero product is an open-source, AI-native email client with MCP tooling: MCP.md lists get-thread-by-ID, send, draft, label, and bulk actions (MCP.md), and the AI router PR adds a /do/:action endpoint for email actions via MCP (PR #1198). For the client problem, Orchid should hand a thread to an agent as a durable, resumable thread object rather than a one-shot prompt: pass thread ID plus message history and labels, keep the agent's draft in a draft state until human approval, and return control to the thread with a visible status so the conversation is never dropped. Required artifacts: a thread-handoff contract (thread ID, message history, labels, permissions, approval gate), an agent status/ownership field on the thread, a draft-and-approve flow, and a sync/return path. Public sources support thread retrieval by ID and draft/send actions (MCP.md) and thread synchronization via the UI (PR #1679), but do not document a formal handoff contract, so the contract shape is an assumption. No source says the company commissioned this work.

experts.opportunities: A durable handoff contract is a differentiator in an agentic email product: it lets Orchid resume threads across sessions and devices, support human-in-the-loop approval as a first-class state, and make agent actions auditable. It also creates a reusable substrate for multiple agents (triage, drafting, scheduling) and for future multi-agent or multi-user handoffs, and it turns 'agent takes the thread' into a testable state machine rather than a demo behavior.

insights.insight: The thread, not the message or the session, must be the durable handoff unit, with a stable thread ID decoupled from provider message IDs.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Email threads mutate: replies arrive, subjects change, providers reassign message IDs, and a human may act mid-handoff. If handoff keys off a message ID or an in-memory agent session, resumption after a crash or a new inbound reply is ambiguous, and the agent can act on a stale view. A stable, Orchid-owned thread ID with an append-only, hash-chained history gives every transition a single referent and lets the agent detect drift (new messages since lease) before acting. This mirrors durable-job patterns where the job record, not the worker session, is the source of truth.
implementation_ideas: Define a ThreadRecord with an Orchid-generated immutable thread_id, a provider_thread_ref kept as a mutable alias, and an append-only message log where each entry stores a content hash and sequence number.
Require every agent action to carry thread_id plus the last-seen sequence number; reject or re-sync actions when the log has advanced.
Add a drift check on lease acquisition and before each send that compares the agent's last-seen sequence to the current head and forces a re-read on mismatch.
identified_risks: Provider thread refs can split or merge (subject changes, forwards), so alias mapping needs reconciliation rules.
Append-only logs grow unbounded and need compaction or snapshotting for long threads.
identified_opportunities: Enables resumable handoff across devices and sessions.
Provides an audit trail for every agent action on a thread.

insights.insight: Approval gates and permissions must be enforced state transitions in the machine, not UI toggles, so a thread cannot be acted on outside its granted scope.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In an agentic email product the dangerous failure is an agent sending or forwarding without human sign-off. If approval is a checkbox in the client, background jobs and retries can bypass it. Modeling 'awaiting-approval' as a state with a required approver identity, and permissions as a capability set attached to the lease (read, draft, send, label, forward), makes the gate checkable server-side on every transition. Idempotent transitions with compare-and-swap on state version prevent double-send when an approval and a retry race.
implementation_ideas: Encode the state machine as a transition table where each edge lists required capabilities and required approver role; reject edges not in the table.
Attach a capability set and TTL to the agent lease; expire the lease and revert to 'returned' if approval is not granted in time.
Use idempotency keys derived from (thread_id, state_version, action) on send and forward so retries cannot duplicate.
identified_risks: Over-strict gates degrade the agent experience and push users to disable approvals.
Approver identity resolution is nontrivial in shared or delegated inboxes.
identified_opportunities: Human-in-the-loop becomes a product feature rather than an afterthought.
Capability-scoped leases allow safe delegation to third-party agents.

insights.insight: Handoff needs an explicit return and escalation path with ownership transfer, so 'agent takes the thread' is reversible and never leaves the thread ownerless.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Agents fail: model timeouts, low confidence, out-of-scope requests. Without a defined 'returned' and 'escalated' state with a named human owner, the thread sits in limbo and the conversation is effectively dropped, which is the client's stated fear. Ownership should be a field on the thread (human owner, agent lease holder, or unassigned queue) changed only by valid transitions, and escalation should notify the owner with the agent's partial work attached. This makes handoff a two-way contract and bounds the blast radius of agent failure.
implementation_ideas: Add 'returned' and 'escalated' states with a required human_owner field and a notification hook carrying the agent's draft and reasoning summary.
Define a lease TTL and heartbeat; on expiry, auto-transition to 'returned' and notify the owner.
Log every ownership change with actor, timestamp, and reason code for audit and replay.
identified_risks: Auto-return on TTL can interrupt a slow but valid agent run.
Escalation noise can train users to ignore notifications.
identified_opportunities: Reversibility builds trust and supports gradual autonomy rollout.
Escalation data reveals where agents fail and guides model and prompt work.

A second risk is silent re-assignment: if agent takeover is modeled as a background action rather than a state transition with an owner, return-to-human and escalation become invisible and unauditable. This creates differentiation around trust and auditability rather than raw automation. It also gives the team reusable artifacts: an ownership state machine, a handoff event log, and a return-to-human escalation contract that other agent features can inherit. experts.recommendation: Model agent takeover as an explicit, visible ownership state transition, not a background action. Ship three artifacts before any autonomous reply: (1) an owner field with enumerated states (human-owned, agent-owned, agent-blocked-needs-human, returned) rendered in the thread header; (2) a handoff event record capturing who handed off, to which agent, why, and the named human return owner; (3) a mandatory escalation contract defining when the agent must flip to agent-blocked-needs-human and notify the return owner. insights.insight: Ownership must be a declared field with enumerated states, never inferred from last activity, because agent and human can act concurrently on one thread.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In collaborative inboxes the failure mode is ambiguity: if ownership is derived from 'who touched it last,' an agent auto-reply and a human reply can interleave and each party assumes the other owns it. A declared owner field makes the current responsible party unambiguous at every moment and gives the UI something concrete to render. This is the same reason assignment fields exist in support tools: accountability must be explicit, not emergent. Without it, 'agent takes a thread' has no durable representation and return/escalation states have nothing to transition from.
implementation_ideas: Add an owner field with values human:<id>, agent:<id>, unassigned, and a separate lifecycle state (owned, handed_off, agent_blocked, returned) so ownership and status are orthogonal.
Render owner and state in the thread header with a colored chip and the named human backstop always visible next to the agent.
Write an invariant check that rejects any agent send when the thread's owner is not that agent or its delegated state.
identified_risks: Migration of existing threads with no owner creates a backfill ambiguity.
Owner field can drift from actual behavior if agents can act without claiming.
identified_opportunities: Owner field becomes the anchor for audit logs, filters, and workload views.
Explicit ownership enables safe parallel human/agent work.

insights.insight: Handoff and return must be first-class, logged state transitions with a named human return owner, so a conversation can never be dropped at the seam.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client problem is specifically 'without dropping the conversation,' and drops happen at transitions, not during steady-state work. If takeover is a background action, there is no record of who gave the thread to the agent, why, or who gets it back. A handoff event (from, to, reason, timestamp, return owner) makes the seam inspectable and reversible. The return owner is the critical field: it guarantees the thread has a human destination when the agent stops, which is exactly what prevents a silent drop.
implementation_ideas: Emit a structured handoff event on every takeover: actor, target agent, reason code, and required return_owner_id.
Require return_owner_id at claim time and block agent activation if it is missing.
Provide a one-click 'return to owner' action that flips state to returned and notifies the return owner with the handoff history attached.
identified_risks: Return owner may be unavailable, recreating a drop; needs a fallback owner rule.
Event volume could clutter the thread if surfaced raw.
identified_opportunities: Handoff log doubles as an audit trail for trust and QA.
Return-owner data enables routing and coverage analytics.

insights.insight: The agent needs an explicit blocked/needs-human escalation state with a defined trigger contract, because escalation is the ownership path back to the human and must be designed, not improvised.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An agent that can take a thread but has no defined way to give up will either stall silently or over-reach. A dedicated agent_blocked state with enumerated triggers (low confidence, missing info, policy boundary, human request) makes escalation a modeled transition rather than an ad hoc behavior. Pairing it with automatic notification to the return owner closes the loop. This mirrors escalation paths in support tools: the value is in the defined trigger and the guaranteed recipient, not in the state label alone.
implementation_ideas: Define an escalation contract listing trigger codes and require the agent to set agent_blocked with a code plus a short reason.
On agent_blocked, auto-notify the return owner and surface the thread at the top of their queue with the blocking reason.
Add a human 'reclaim' control available at all times that forces state to returned regardless of agent state.
identified_risks: Agents may over-escalate or under-escalate if triggers are vague.
Auto-notification could spam the return owner without batching.
identified_opportunities: Escalation telemetry reveals where agents need better context.
A reliable escalation path increases willingness to delegate.

experts.name: Dana Kessler

experts.lens: Keeps drafts as drafts: specifies the approval gate, what the agent may touch before approval, and how approved drafts convert to sends without losing thread context.

The core risk is that a thread handed to an agent loses its conversational spine: if the agent drafts outside the thread's native context (participants, prior messages, attachments, labels), the eventual send either forks the conversation or requires a human to re-paste context. experts.opportunities: An approval-first handoff is a differentiator precisely because public agent-email products tend to emphasize autonomy. Orchid can make the draft-until-approved loop the visible contract: the agent may read the thread, assemble context, and produce a draft, but the send is gated on an explicit human approval that is bound to the draft revision. This preserves thread continuity by construction, since the draft lives inside the thread and the approved artifact converts to a send in place. experts.recommendation: Adopt a single handoff contract: the agent receives a frozen thread envelope (participants, message history, attachments, labels, and the human's stated intent) and may only produce draft revisions inside that envelope. Nothing leaves the draft state until a human approves a specific revision; approval binds to that revision hash, and the approved revision converts to a send in the same thread with context intact. Ship the four artifacts (envelope, revision, approval record, send receipt) before shipping any agent autonomy beyond drafting.

insights.insight: The approval gate should bind to a specific draft revision, not to the thread, so that edits after approval cannot silently ride along on an earlier yes.
insights.supporting_reasoning: If approval attaches to the thread or to the agent session, any post-approval edit by the agent or a collaborator converts an approved draft into an unapproved one without a new decision. Revision-bound approval makes the gate meaningful: the human approves exactly the bytes that will send, and any subsequent change reopens the gate. This is the difference between a real approval-first loop and a ceremonial one, and it is the mechanism that keeps the draft a draft until the last responsible moment.
implementation_ideas: Hash each draft revision and store the hash in the approval record so the send step verifies the approved revision matches the outgoing body
Invalidate the approval state automatically on any edit to subject, body, recipients, or attachments and surface a re-approval prompt in the thread
Show a diff between the approved revision and the current revision when re-approval is triggered so the human sees only what changed
identified_risks: Re-approval friction on trivial edits may train users to approve without reading
Hash verification adds a failure mode if the send pipeline mutates the body after approval (for example signature injection)
identified_opportunities: A visible revision-bound gate becomes a trust signal Orchid can describe publicly without claiming autonomy
Revision history doubles as an audit trail for disputed sends

insights.insight: The handoff envelope must be frozen at handoff time and carried through to send, so the agent drafts against a stable thread snapshot rather than a moving conversation.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Threads mutate while an agent works: new replies arrive, labels change, attachments are added. If the agent reads live state, its draft can reference context the approver never saw, or miss a reply that arrived mid-draft. Freezing the envelope at handoff gives the agent a defined input, gives the approver a defined basis for judgment, and gives the send step a defined context to reattach to. On approval, the system reconciles the frozen envelope against the live thread and flags divergence (new messages, changed participants) before sending, so continuity is preserved rather than assumed.
implementation_ideas: Capture the envelope as an immutable record at handoff: message IDs, participants, attachment references, labels, and the human's intent string
On approval, diff the frozen envelope against live thread state and block send with a reconciliation prompt if participants or message count changed
Reattach the approved draft to the live thread by message ID rather than by subject line so threading survives replies that arrived during drafting
identified_risks: Blocking on divergence can stall sends during fast-moving threads
Envelope snapshots duplicate message content and raise storage and retention questions
identified_opportunities: Divergence detection is a defensible feature public pages of competitors rarely describe
Frozen envelopes make agent behavior reproducible for debugging

insights.insight: The team needs a send receipt that references the approved revision and the envelope, so an approved draft converts to a send without severing the thread's provenance.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Conversion from draft to send is where thread context is most often lost: a naive implementation composes a new message from the draft body, dropping in-reply-to headers, references, and the envelope linkage. A receipt object that records envelope ID, approved revision hash, approver, timestamp, and the resulting sent message ID keeps the chain intact and makes the send auditable and reversible in description. It also gives the team a concrete artifact to test against, which is more reliable than prose requirements about 'keeping context'.
implementation_ideas: Emit a send receipt on conversion containing envelope ID, revision hash, approver identity, timestamp, and sent message ID, stored alongside the thread
Derive in-reply-to and references headers from the envelope's last message ID at send time rather than from the draft body
Expose the receipt in the thread UI as a compact 'approved by X, sent at Y' line linking to the approved revision
identified_risks: Receipts that store approver identity create a visible accountability surface some users may resist
Header derivation bugs would mis-thread sends in a way that is hard to notice until replies scatter
identified_opportunities: Receipts support later features like recall, resend, and approval analytics without schema changes
A visible approval line in-thread reinforces the draft-until-approved contract to every participant

insights.insight: Thread identity must be a stable, shared ID that both the UI and the agent reference; the agent should never operate on a copied thread body.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The return leg only works if there is one canonical thing to re-sync to. If the client hands over a snapshot and the agent mutates its own copy, the UI has no key to reconcile against and the conversation forks into two truths. Retrieval-by-ID is the natural sync primitive in MCP-style tooling, so making the ID the contract aligns the handoff and the return path around the same anchor. This is a design inference from how ID-based retrieval composes, not a claim about Orchid's internals.
implementation_ideas: Define a handoff manifest carrying thread_id, owner, scope, expiry, and allowed_actions; the agent must echo thread_id on every event.
Make the client re-fetch the thread by ID on each return-path event and diff against its local view before rendering.
Reject agent events whose thread_id doesn't match the active handoff, and surface a mismatch as a visible error rather than a silent merge.
identified_risks: Thread ID reuse or mutation across clients breaks reconciliation.
Agent tooling that only supports body-copy handoff forces an adapter layer.
identified_opportunities: One ID-keyed contract supports web and mobile clients with the same return path.
Deterministic diffing enables safe retries and audit trails.

insights.insight: Control return should be an explicit, observable state transition with a defined handback trigger, not an inferred timeout.
insights.supporting_reasoning: If the client can't tell 'agent working' from 'agent done' from 'agent failed', drafts and sends race the human and the thread view lies about who owns it. Modeling owner state (human / agent / returning) and requiring the agent to emit a terminal event (returned or failed) makes handback legible and testable. A timeout can be a backstop, but as the primary trigger it produces ambiguous states and stale ownership. This follows from the return-leg lens: clean control return is a protocol, not an absence of activity.
implementation_ideas: Add an owner field to thread state with explicit transitions and render each state distinctly in the UI.
Require a terminal return-path event (returned/failed) before the client re-enables human editing and send.
Use a timeout only as a backstop that forces the thread into 'returning' and flags it for human review, never straight to 'human'.
identified_risks: Agents that crash without emitting a terminal event leave threads stuck in 'agent'.
Extra state transitions add UI complexity and edge cases.
identified_opportunities: Legible ownership builds user trust in delegation.
Explicit handback makes the loop testable end to end.

insights.insight: Draft and send must be idempotent, ID-keyed operations so re-syncs and retries never duplicate or orphan messages.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The return leg re-fetches and may retry; if draft and send aren't idempotent, a retried send produces duplicates and a re-synced draft can orphan the human's edit. Keying both operations by thread ID plus an idempotency key lets the client safely replay and reconcile. Composing draft-then-send as separate, confirmable steps also keeps the human in the loop before anything leaves the mailbox. This is a reliability inference from how retry-prone sync loops behave.
implementation_ideas: Attach an idempotency key to every draft and send call; the server dedupes on (thread_id, idempotency_key).
Land agent drafts in the thread as reviewable drafts and gate send behind explicit human or policy confirmation.
On re-sync, match drafts by idempotency key and merge rather than overwrite human edits.
identified_risks: Dedupe state must persist across client restarts or retries still duplicate.
Gating every send on confirmation slows high-volume threads.
identified_opportunities: Safe retries make the sync loop robust to flaky networks.
Reviewable drafts give a natural human-in-the-loop checkpoint.

experts.name: Amara Sotelo
experts.background: Research analyst who separates documented behavior from assumption, working only from public pages such as llms.txt, the FAQ, MCP.md, and referenced PRs.
experts.lens: Flags what public sources actually support (thread retrieval, draft/send, UI sync) versus what the handoff contract must assume, and keeps claims free of commissioning language.
experts.risks: Public sources (llms.txt, FAQ, MCP.md, referenced PRs) describe capabilities in isolation, so the handoff contract risks encoding assumptions the public record never confirms: that thread retrieval is complete and stable, that draft/send is a single atomic action, and that UI sync reflects agent state in real time. If any of these are only partially documented, the contract will over-promise. A second risk is provenance drift: pages may be stale or describe intended rather than shipped behavior, and PRs show code intent, not runtime guarantees. A third risk is that 'handoff' is never defined p
experts.opportunities: Public pages give a defensible baseline: the contract can be scoped to only what llms.txt, FAQ, and MCP.md actually state, with explicit 'assumed' markers for everything else. Referenced PRs offer a paper trail for reviewable claims. This lets the team build a handoff artifact set (thread snapshot, authority grant, sync acknowledgment) that is auditable and easy to revise as public documentation changes, and keeps claims free of commissioning language.
experts.recommendation: Build the handoff contract as a two-layer document: a 'Documented' layer citing exact public pages/PRs for thread retrieval, draft/send, and UI sync, and an 'Assumed' layer listing every gap the team must validate before relying on it. Ship three artifacts: a thread-context snapshot schema, an explicit authority grant (read/draft/send) with a named approver, and a sync-acknowledgment event the UI must emit before the agent proceeds. Treat any capability not found in public sources as unverified until confirmed.

insights.insight: Thread retrieval should be treated as a snapshot-plus-delta contract, not a live stream, because public sources do not document real-time continuity guarantees.
insights.supporting_reasoning: llms.txt, FAQ, and MCP.md describe retrieval and tool surfaces but the public record does not establish that an agent receives continuous thread updates. A handoff that assumes a live feed will silently drop messages arriving mid-task. Designing for a snapshot with an explicit delta/re-fetch step keeps the contract honest to what is documented and degrades safely if live sync is absent.
implementation_ideas: Define a thread snapshot object (message IDs, ordering, timestamps) captured at handoff time.
Require a re-fetch/delta check before any draft or send action.
Log snapshot version and delta results so gaps are visible in review.
identified_risks: Snapshot may miss messages sent between capture and agent action.
Public pages may not specify ordering or pagination semantics.
identified_opportunities: Auditable trail of exactly what context the agent held.
Safe behavior even if live sync is undocumented.

insights.insight: Draft and send must be separate, explicitly granted authorities, because public sources do not show a single atomic draft-and-send primitive.
insights.supporting_reasoning: MCP.md and FAQ describe drafting and sending as distinct surfaces; nothing public confirms they are transactional. If the contract bundles them, a failed send leaves ambiguous state. Splitting authority into read, draft, and send, each with a named approver and a confirmation step, matches the documented surface and makes failure modes legible.
implementation_ideas: Encode authority as a grant object with read/draft/send flags and an approver identity.
Require an explicit confirm event between draft and send.
Record draft ID and send receipt separately in the handoff log.
identified_risks: Extra confirmation adds latency the product may not want.
Public sources may not define send receipts, forcing an assumption.
identified_opportunities: Clear accountability for who authorized a send.
Reusable grant model across future agent tasks.

insights.insight: UI sync should be a required acknowledgment event before the agent acts, because public pages describe UI state but not guaranteed propagation to the agent.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The FAQ and referenced PRs touch UI behavior, yet the public record does not establish that agent-visible state and UI state converge. Without an ack, the agent may act on stale context while the user sees a different thread. Making sync an explicit event the UI emits turns an implicit assumption into a testable contract point and surfaces divergence early.
implementation_ideas: Define a sync-ack event carrying thread version and UI timestamp.
Block draft/send until the latest ack matches the snapshot version.
Surface mismatches to the user as a visible warning rather than silent retry.
identified_risks: Ack semantics are inferred, not documented, so the event may not map to real UI behavior.
Blocking on ack could stall handoff if the UI never emits it.
identified_opportunities: Divergence becomes observable and reviewable.
Contract stays honest about what sync actually guarantees.

experts.name: Lena Vossberg

insights.insight: Handoff must be a compare-and-swap ownership transition on a durable thread object, not a prompt handoff.
insights.supporting_reasoning: If the agent 'takes' a thread by being handed a rendered prompt, the thread's real state lives in the prompt and diverges from the mailbox on the next inbound message, retry, or human edit. A durable object with an ownership field and a CAS transition (expected_version -> new owner) makes concurrent claims deterministic: exactly one claimant wins, the loser gets a stale-version error and re-reads. This mirrors how sync layers already resolve conflicting flag/state writes and is the only way handoff survives reconnects and duplicate delivery.
implementation_ideas: Add an ownership field (owner_type: human|agent|none, owner_id, lease_expiry, version) to the thread record; handoff is a CAS write on version.
Require an idempotency key per handoff request so retried API calls do not double-assign or re-trigger the agent.
Emit an ownership_changed event to the append-only log on every transition, including failed CAS attempts, for audit.
identified_risks: CAS adds latency and a failure path the UI must handle gracefully.
Lease expiry can strand a thread if the agent crashes without releasing.
identified_opportunities: Deterministic conflict resolution enables multi-agent and multi-human collaboration on the same mailbox.
Audit trail supports compliance and debugging of who held a thread when.

insights.insight: The agent must receive a versioned context bundle pinned to a log offset, not a mutable snapshot.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A snapshot goes stale the moment a new message arrives or a human edits a draft. Pinning the bundle to a log offset (bundle = thread_id + offset + rendered context) lets the agent detect drift: if the thread's current offset exceeds the bundle's, the agent re-fetches or aborts. This is the same resumability principle as resumable sync cursors; it makes agent actions reproducible and lets the team replay exactly what the agent saw when it acted.
implementation_ideas: Define a context-bundle schema with thread_id, log_offset, message set, and policy flags; store bundles immutably.
Have the agent echo the bundle offset on every action so the server can reject stale writes.
Provide a re-fetch endpoint that returns only events after the bundle offset for cheap catch-up.
identified_risks: Storing every bundle grows storage; needs retention policy.
Agents that ignore offset checks can still act on stale context.
identified_opportunities: Replayable bundles make agent behavior debuggable and testable.
Offset-based catch-up is cheaper than full re-render on every turn.

insights.insight: Thread identity must be provider-agnostic and split/merge-aware, or handoff will attach to the wrong conversation.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Message-ID/References are the durable threading signal, but providers rewrite headers, subjects change, and some clients omit References. A thread_id derived only from the latest Message-ID breaks on split; one derived only from subject merges unrelated threads. The robust approach is a normalized root-ID with an explicit split/merge event model: when References indicates a new root, fork a new thread_id and log the split; when a reply re-joins, log a merge with a pointer. Handoff then targets a thread_id that is stable across provider quirks.
implementation_ideas: Derive thread_id from the normalized References root with a hashed fallback when headers are absent; never from subject alone.
Log split and merge events with pointers to the prior thread_id so history is preserved.
Add a reconciliation job that flags threads whose header chain contradicts their assigned thread_id.
identified_risks: Header rewriting by providers can produce false splits.
Merge logic can resurrect closed threads unexpectedly.
identified_opportunities: Correct threading improves agent context quality and reduces wrong-thread replies.
Split/merge history is valuable for support analytics.

insights.insight: The handoff should be a typed, versioned interface object, not a UI action or a prompt convention.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public descriptions of agentic inboxes treat takeover as a product behavior, which hides the contract. If the handoff is only a button, the thread ID, permission scope, and return path live in client state and are lost on reload or runtime restart. A versioned schema forces the team to name every field the runtime needs and lets the approval gate and return path be validated server-side. It also makes the contract reviewable and testable independent of the model.
implementation_ideas: Write a HandoffRequest JSON schema with required fields thread_id, actor_id, scope, approval_gate, return_path, and contract_version; reject requests missing any field.
Store the active handoff as a server-side record keyed by thread_id so client reloads cannot orphan it.
Add schema conformance tests with fixture threads covering missing scope, expired return path, and unknown contract_version.
identified_risks: Schema churn breaks in-flight handoffs if contract_version is not enforced.
Overly rigid schema slows iteration on new agent capabilities.
identified_opportunities: The schema doubles as public documentation and an MCP tool boundary.
Versioning enables safe rollout of new gate modes.

insights.insight: The approval gate must be server-enforced state with an explicit enum, not a client-side toggle.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An agent that can send email needs a gate the runtime cannot skip. If approval lives in the UI, any new tool call path or runtime restart can bypass it. Encoding the gate as an enum in the handoff record and checking it in the send endpoint makes bypass a server error rather than a silent behavior. The enum also lets the product express graduated trust: auto for low-risk drafts, human-approve-before-send for outbound, human-approve-on-uncertain for ambiguous threads.
implementation_ideas: Add approval_gate to the handoff record and enforce it in the send endpoint: reject sends when gate is human-approve-before-send and no approval event exists.
Emit an ApprovalEvent with approver_id and timestamp that the send endpoint checks transactionally.
Default new handoffs to human-approve-before-send and require an explicit downgrade to auto.
identified_risks: Approval latency stalls threads the agent could have handled.
Approvers may rubber-stamp, eroding the gate's value.
identified_opportunities: Graduated gates build user trust incrementally.
Approval events create an audit trail for compliance.

insights.insight: The return path must be mandatory and guaranteed: every handoff ends with a HandoffReturn that reassigns the thread to the human.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The failure mode that drops conversations is an agent that takes a thread and never gives it back on error, timeout, or low confidence. Making return_path a required field with explicit timeout and failure semantics means the runtime has a defined exit for every branch. A HandoffReturn event that reassigns ownership to the human thread closes the loop and makes the handoff auditable. Without it, the contract is one-directional and the human is left guessing who owns the thread.
implementation_ideas: Require return_path with timeout_seconds and on_failure enum (return_to_human, escalate, park) in every HandoffRequest.
Have the runtime emit a HandoffReturn event on completion, error, timeout, or confidence below threshold, reassigning thread ownership.
Add a watchdog that fires HandoffReturn if no agent heartbeat arrives within timeout_seconds.
identified_risks: Aggressive timeouts return threads mid-task and frustrate users.
Watchdog bugs could reassign threads the agent is actively working.
identified_opportunities: Guaranteed return makes agent takeover safe to try.
Return events give clean data on where agents fail.

insights.insight: Ownership must be visible on the thread itself, not inferred from behavior, or the conversation feels dropped the moment the agent takes over.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In approval-first interfaces the counterpart and the human sender both read the thread as a social contract. When an agent acts without a visible status, people fill the gap with latency and tone cues, and after any surprise send they rebuild trust slowly. A thread-level status that names the human owner and the agent's current state keeps the contract legible, so a pause reads as 'drafting, awaiting approval' rather than 'abandoned'. This is a design inference from diary-style observation of recovery, not a measured result.
implementation_ideas: Add a thread header status showing the named human owner and an agent state chip (idle, drafting, awaiting approval).
Make handoff an explicit, reversible action that writes an owner stamp into the thread timeline.
Show the same status to the counterpart as a lightweight indicator so a pause is explained, not guessed.
identified_risks: Status chips can go stale and mislead if not tied to real agent state.
Showing agent status to the counterpart may raise expectations of speed the agent cannot meet.
Owner stamps can be reassigned silently, recreating the invisibility problem.
identified_opportunities: Status becomes the trust surface that lets the team widen autonomy safely.
Visible ownership reduces 'did anyone see this?' anxiety and stalled threads.
The status component is reusable across every agent-assisted flow.

insights.insight: Drafts must stay drafts until a human approves, with the draft state rendered as a visible artifact rather than a hidden convention.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client problem is handing off without dropping the conversation, and the failure mode is an agent send that surprises the human. If drafts look like sent mail, the human cannot tell what is still theirs to change. Rendering drafts with a persistent draft status, and gating send behind an explicit approval, keeps the human as the author of record. The team also needs the draft-with-status as a reviewable artifact so design and engineering share one definition of 'still a draft'.
implementation_ideas: Render agent output in a distinct draft state with a status chip that persists until approval.
Require an explicit approve action before send, with edit-then-approve as the default path.
Log each draft revision and approval on the thread so the draft's history is inspectable.
identified_risks: Extra approval steps can slow replies and tempt users to auto-approve.
A draft chip that is easy to miss still permits surprise sends.
Approval fatigue may erode the gate over time.
identified_opportunities: Draft-status clarity is the clearest expression of the approval-first promise.
The draft component doubles as the team's shared review artifact.
Edit-then-approve captures human corrections as signal for the agent.

insights.insight: The team needs a handoff record and an approval log as first-class artifacts, or the 'never dropped' guarantee lives only in people's heads.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A handoff without a record cannot be audited, reversed, or reviewed in a diary study. The artifacts the team needs are the same ones that make the flow legible: a handoff record (who handed off, when, to which agent state), a draft-with-status component, and an approval log (who approved or edited what). Together they let the team observe recovery after surprise actions and let users see the thread's history. This follows from the ownership-and-status lens rather than from any published metric.
implementation_ideas: Define a handoff record schema capturing owner, timestamp, agent state, and reversal.
Keep an approval log on the thread showing approvals and edits with actor and time.
Run a diary study where senders log reactions after agent actions, reviewed against the approval log.
identified_risks: Logs add surface area and can leak detail users did not expect to see.
Artifacts can be built but ignored if not surfaced in the thread UI.
Diary study findings may not generalize beyond the pilot.
identified_opportunities: Artifacts make the flow auditable and reversible, supporting wider autonomy.
The approval log feeds agent improvement with real human corrections.
Shared artifacts align design and engineering on one definition of handoff.

Acceptance criteria can assert that every thread has exactly one owner and one status at all times.

Add a required owner/status field to the thread model with a validation rule that rejects ownerless threads.
Write acceptance criteria: no thread may sit in agent-drafting without a timestamped agent action, and every transition is logged.

insights.insight: Draft-and-approve is the safe default handoff mode; full autonomy should be opt-in per thread.

Add a per-thread autonomy toggle that skips approval only when explicitly enabled.
Write acceptance criteria: an agent draft cannot send while in awaiting-approval, and approval or rejection returns the thread to a named human.
identified_risks: Approval queue can bottleneck and stall threads if notifications fail.
Users may toggle autonomy on and forget, reintroducing drop risk.
identified_opportunities: Approval gate builds trust and gives a clean return-to-human trigger.
Rejection reasons become training signal for agent drafts.

insights.insight: The return path must be explicit and context-preserving so a handed-off thread can always come back to a human.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A handoff without a return path is a one-way door and the main cause of dropped conversations. The agent needs defined triggers to hand back (low confidence, approval rejection, timeout, human takeover) and must return with context intact. This is testable: every return must restore human ownership and carry the agent's draft and notes. Public pages do not specify this, so it belongs in the contract as an open item resolved before build.

Require the return action to set owner to the named human and attach the agent's draft plus a summary note.
Write acceptance criteria: after any return, status is human-owned, the human is notified, and no agent action fires until re-handed.
identified_risks: Timeout thresholds are guesses without public data and may return too early or late.
Context notes can be noisy and bury the human in agent output.
identified_opportunities: Explicit return path eliminates the one-way-door failure mode.
Return notes give the human a fast catch-up summary.

insights.insight: The only defensible handoff design is one built on re-retrieval by thread ID plus draft-before-send, because those are the primitives the public pages actually name; continuity should be engineered as repeated re-read, not as an assumed persistent session.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public Orchid/Zero/Mail0 material describes thread-by-ID retrieval, draft/send actions, and UI sync, but publishes no session, lease, or ownership-transfer model. Designing as if sync resolves conflicts overruns the sources; designing a human confirmation gate and a re-read check keeps the design honest while the semantics are unknown.

Instrument the demo to record whether agent drafts appear in the UI and how fast, as observed behavior distinct from documented behavior.
Add a conflict question to the unknowns register: what happens when human and agent act on the same thread concurrently.

Observed-vs-documented instrumentation produces concrete questions for the vendor.

Cross-generation diff showing which primitives appear under Zero, Mail0, and Orchid, flagging any that appear only once.
Rule that no contract field ships without either a pinned source or an ASSUMED tag with an owner.

Generation labeling is itself inferred from rename history and could mislabel a page.
identified_opportunities: Cross-generation stability becomes a defensible confidence input.
The evidence map is reusable for future vendor audits.

insights.insight: A thread must be a durable object with a stable ID before any handoff is allowed; the handoff is a transition on that object, not a mode toggle.
insights.supporting_reasoning: If the thread identity is implicit or derived from mutable fields (subject, participants, latest message), a crash or concurrent edit during handoff can re-key the thread and orphan the agent's context. This is the precondition for every other guarantee; without it, idempotency and resumability have nothing stable to attach to.
implementation_ideas: Assign an immutable thread ID at thread creation and never derive it from subject/participants; carry it through every message and transition.
Store ownership as a field on the thread record with a monotonically increasing transition sequence number.
Reject any agent action whose thread ID or transition sequence does not match the committed ownership record.
identified_risks: Legacy threads without stable IDs need a backfill/mapping step before they can be handed off.
A stable ID that leaks into user-visible surfaces can be confused with message IDs.
identified_opportunities: Stable IDs make agent actions auditable and reversible per thread.
Enables safe concurrent human edit because edits target a known object.

insights.insight: Handoff must be idempotent: a retried or duplicated handoff request must converge to exactly one ownership transition.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Handoffs will be retried on timeout, double-clicked, and replayed after crash. Without an idempotency key, the system can double-take, flip ownership twice, or spawn two agent runs on one thread. An idempotent token keyed to (thread ID, transition) makes retry safe and lets the client retry freely. This is the crash-and-retry answer the lens demands before any handoff is allowed.
implementation_ideas: Issue a client-generated idempotency key per handoff attempt; store it with the transition and return the prior result on replay.
Make the ownership transition a compare-and-set on the current state so a stale duplicate is a no-op.
Log every handoff attempt with its key and outcome so duplicates are visible and diagnosable.
identified_risks: Key scope too broad can suppress a legitimate second handoff; scope must include the transition, not just the thread.
Stored keys need expiry/retention policy or they accumulate.
identified_opportunities: Safe client retry improves perceived reliability.
Attempt logs become an audit trail for agent actions.

insights.insight: The handoff is a resumable state machine with a durable checkpoint, and ownership is single-writer per state so concurrent human edit cannot race the agent.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A handoff can block on external calls or crash mid-transition. If state lives only in memory or the UI, an interrupted handoff restarts from scratch or leaves ownership ambiguous. A durable checkpoint lets it resume at the last committed step. Single-writer-per-state plus an explicit handoff-back state resolves the concurrent-edit case: while handoff-pending or agent-owned, human edits either queue or force a defined transition back, never a silent dual-write.
implementation_ideas: Persist each handoff step with a checkpoint record so an interrupted handoff resumes at the last committed step, not the start.
Enforce single-writer per state; a human edit during agent-owned triggers an explicit handoff-back transition rather than a parallel write.
Define and test crash points (before commit, after commit, mid-agent-run) with resume behavior specified for each.
identified_risks: More states mean more transitions to test; an under-specified handoff-back can strand a thread.
Checkpoint storage adds write load on a hot path.
identified_opportunities: Resumability makes long or blocked handoffs reliable.
Explicit handoff-back gives users a clear escape hatch and builds trust.

experts.name: Desmond Achebe
experts.background: Designed draft-and-approve review queues for regulated outbound communications and open-source review tooling; publishes on approval gates, diffable drafts, and audit trails that keep a human as the final sender.
experts.lens: Insists every agent action lands as a reviewable artifact with a visible pending state; maps exactly where approval gates sit so drafts never silently become sends.
experts.risks: Public pages for Orchid (orchid.ai), formerly Zero and Mail0, describe an agentic email product but do not, from what is publicly visible, specify the approval-gate model, the pending-state UI, or the audit trail. The core risk is therefore a handoff that is technically seamless but governance-blind: the agent takes the thread, drafts or sends, and the human loses the exact point where a draft became a send. Secondary risks: (1) the rebrand from Zero/Mail0 means public documentation may lag the product, so any design inferred from public pages can be stale; (2) an agent 'taking a thread' is am
experts.opportunities: A handoff designed as a reviewable artifact rather than a mode switch differentiates Orchid: every agent takeover produces a visible pending card in the thread with the agent's proposed next action, the diff against the last human message, and an explicit approve/edit/reject gate before send. Because the product is early and public docs are thin, Orchid can define the handoff contract publicly and make it a trust feature. Diffable drafts and a per-thread audit log are cheap to build relative to their credibility value with regulated senders. The rebrand is also an opportunity to publish a clea
experts.recommendation: Make the handoff a first-class, reviewable artifact: when an agent takes a thread, insert a visible 'Agent has the thread — pending' state into the thread itself, with the agent's proposed action, a diffable draft, the preserved thread context (participants, CC/BCC, attachments, quoted history), and a single approval gate that is the only path to send. The team needs three artifacts: (a) a handoff record (who handed off, when, scope: read/draft/send), (b) a diffable draft artifact with a pending badge, and (c) an append-only audit log entry per state change. Until public docs confirm these exi

insights.insight: The handoff, not the agent, should be the artifact: a thread takeover must land as a visible pending record in the conversation before any draft or send occurs.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In draft-and-approve systems the failure mode is not a bad draft but an invisible transition — the moment the agent assumes control is exactly where a human loses the ability to intervene. If the handoff is a mode toggle in settings, the thread looks identical before and after takeover, and the human cannot tell whether the agent is reading, drafting, or about to send. Making the handoff an in-thread artifact with an explicit scope (read-only, draft-only, draft-and-send-on-approval) forces the authorization question to be answered at the point of takeover rather than assumed. This mirrors the regulated-outbound pattern where the gate sits between draft and send and every state change is recorded. Public Orchid pages describe an agentic email product but do not evidence this artifact, so it is a design gap to close, not a confirmed feature.
implementation_ideas: Insert a system-authored 'Agent has the thread' card into the thread with fields: handing-off user, timestamp, scope (read/draft/send), and the agent's stated intent for the next message.
Render the card as a pending state with a distinct visual badge that persists until a human approves, edits, or revokes the handoff.
Require scope selection at handoff time and block send if scope is read-only or draft-only, surfacing the block in the card.
identified_risks: Card clutter in long threads if every takeover and revocation is inlined.
Users may click through the handoff card without reading scope, recreating the silent-send problem.
Scope vocabulary (read/draft/send) may confuse non-technical senders.
identified_opportunities: The handoff card becomes a shareable trust artifact for regulated teams.
Scope-at-handoff gives Orchid a clean authorization model to document publicly.
Revocation becomes a first-class action rather than an implicit setting change.

insights.insight: Drafts must be diffable against the last human message so approval is a comparison, not a blank-page read.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An approver who reads an agent draft cold is reviewing prose; an approver who sees a diff against the prior human message is reviewing a change, which is faster and catches dropped context — removed CCs, trimmed quoted history, altered commitments. Diffable drafts also make the approval gate meaningful: the human approves a specific delta, and the audit log can store the exact diff that was approved. This is the pattern from open-source review tooling applied to outbound mail, and it is the strongest defense against the agent silently dropping thread state at handoff. Public pages do not show a diff view, so this is inferred design rather than confirmed behavior.
implementation_ideas: Store the agent draft as a structured delta against the last human message: body changes, participant changes, attachment changes, and quoted-history changes each shown separately.
Show a side-by-side or inline diff in the pending draft with per-hunk accept/reject.
Persist the approved diff hash in the audit log so the sent message is provably the reviewed one.
identified_risks: Diff noise on heavily reformatted drafts can bury the substantive change.
Approvers may accept hunks without reading, giving false assurance.
Diffing quoted history and attachments is more complex than diffing body text.
identified_opportunities: Diff review is a credible differentiator for regulated outbound communications.
Per-hunk accept/reject gives fine-grained human control without rejecting the whole draft.
Approved-diff hashing supports later audit and dispute resolution.

insights.insight: The team needs an append-only audit log keyed to the thread, recording handoff, draft, approval, edit, and send as discrete events.
insights.supporting_reasoning: If the only record of an agent action is the resulting email, the human cannot reconstruct who authorized what. A per-thread event log — handoff scope, draft version, approver identity, edit, send, revocation — makes the approval gate auditable and lets the team debug dropped-context incidents after the fact. It also turns the pending state from a UI convention into an enforceable record: a send without a preceding approval event is detectable. Regulated senders need this, and it is the artifact most likely to be missing when a product ships an agent fast. Public Orchid pages do not evidence an audit log, so this is a gap to specify before handoff ships.
implementation_ideas: Emit a structured event per state change (handoff, draft_created, draft_edited, approved, sent, revoked) with actor, timestamp, thread id, and diff hash.
Expose the log as a per-thread timeline visible to thread participants and exportable for compliance review.
Make send conditional on a preceding approval event for the current draft version, failing closed if the log is missing an entry.
identified_risks: Log volume and retention cost grow with thread activity.
Export formats may not match a customer's compliance tooling.
Fail-closed send on missing log entries can block legitimate sends if logging breaks.
identified_opportunities: Audit export becomes an enterprise selling point.
The log supports incident review when context is dropped at handoff.
Fail-closed send enforces the gate by construction rather than by convention.

experts.name: Wren Takahashi
experts.role: Agent orchestration and MCP tooling engineer
experts.background: Built tool-calling routers and MCP server integrations for email actions, including action endpoints, permission scoping, and return-to-caller control flow; active in open-source agent tooling discussions.
experts.lens: Focuses on the handoff contract as an API surface: what the agent receives, what it may call, how control returns to the thread, and how failures degrade to a safe draft.
experts.risks: Public pages describe Orchid (formerly Zero/Mail0) as an AI-forward email product, but the handoff contract between thread and agent is not documented publicly, so any design here is inference from the product category, not from Orchid's stated architecture. The core risk is an underspecified contract: if the agent receives a thread as an opaque blob with implicit permissions, the team cannot reason about what the agent saw, what it may send, or how the human regains control. A second risk is silent takeover — the agent acts on a thread while the human still believes they hold it, producing du
experts.opportunities: Treating the handoff as an explicit API surface — a thread-handoff object with a scoped capability token, a return-to-caller channel, and a draft-on-failure default — makes the agent's authority auditable and revocable, which is a differentiator in a category where trust is the bottleneck. A well-specified contract also lets the team build deterministic tests: replay a thread, assert the agent's allowed calls, assert control returns to the human on timeout or error. Scoped, thread-level grants open the door to multi-agent or third-party tool use without mailbox-wide exposure. A draft-first deg
experts.recommendation: Define the handoff as a versioned contract before writing agent code: a ThreadHandoff object carrying thread id, message history reference, the acting identity, an explicit capability scope (read thread, draft, send-with-approval, send-direct), a return-to-caller handle, and a failure policy that defaults to producing a draft and pausing. Ship it behind a feature flag with a kill switch that revokes the scope and returns control to the human thread owner. Build the artifacts the team needs around that contract: a schema doc, a permission matrix, a replayable test fixture set, and an audit log

insights.insight: The handoff should be modeled as a scoped, expiring capability grant rather than a role the agent assumes, so control return is a revocation, not a negotiation.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In tool-calling routers the failure mode that hurts most is ambient authority: the agent can act anywhere in the mailbox because it authenticated as the user. If the handoff instead mints a thread-scoped token listing exactly the calls permitted (read, draft, send), then returning control is a single revoke, and every action is attributable to a handoff id. This also makes the human's re-entry unambiguous — the token is dead, so any late agent call fails closed rather than racing the human. The contract becomes testable: assert that after return, a send call is rejected.
implementation_ideas: Mint a handoff id plus a capability token enumerating allowed tool calls and the target thread id; reject any call outside the enumeration.
Expire the token on explicit return, on human reply, and on a max wall-clock TTL, whichever comes first.
Log every tool call against the handoff id so the audit trail shows exactly what the agent did under which grant.
identified_risks: Token plumbing adds latency and a new failure point on every agent call.
If expiry races an in-flight send, the agent may fail after composing, wasting work unless the draft is preserved.
identified_opportunities: Revocable grants make third-party or multi-agent tool use safe without mailbox-wide exposure.
A clean revocation path is a trust feature the team can demo and test deterministically.

insights.insight: Control must return to the caller through an explicit channel with a defined terminal state, not by the agent going quiet.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An agent that simply stops calling tools is indistinguishable from one that crashed, and the human cannot tell whether to wait or take over. The handoff contract needs a return-to-caller signal carrying a terminal reason — done, needs-approval, blocked, error — plus the artifact produced (draft id or sent message id). This mirrors return-to-caller control flow in router design: the caller always gets a typed result, never silence. With a typed terminal state the UI can render the right affordance (review draft, resume thread) and the team can assert on it in tests. Silence as a state is the bug.
implementation_ideas: Define an enum of terminal reasons and require exactly one on every return; treat missing return as a timeout handled by the failure policy.
Have the return payload carry the produced artifact reference (draft id or message id) so the human lands on something concrete.
Add a watchdog that fires the timeout return if no terminal signal arrives within the thread's budget.
identified_risks: A required terminal signal can be dropped by a crashing agent, so the watchdog is load-bearing and must itself be tested.
Overly granular terminal reasons leak agent internals into the human UI.
identified_opportunities: Typed returns make the handoff replayable in tests and observable in production.
Clear terminal states reduce human hesitation about whether to take the thread back.

insights.insight: Failure should degrade to a reviewable draft and a paused thread, never to a sent message or a dead thread.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The worst outcomes in an email handoff are an unsanctioned send and a conversation that stalls with no artifact. A draft-on-failure default bounds both: the agent's partial work is preserved as a draft, the thread is marked paused, and the human is handed back control with something to edit. This is the safe-degradation principle applied to the contract — every error path (tool failure, timeout, permission denial, ambiguous intent) routes to the same terminal state. It also means send-with-approval can be the default scope and send-direct an opt-in, so early deployments cannot send wrongly. The draft is the artifact that makes failure recoverable rather than costly.
implementation_ideas: Route every error class to a single degrade function that writes the current composition as a draft and returns a paused terminal state.
Default new handoffs to draft-plus-approval scope; require an explicit flag to grant send-direct.
Surface the degrade reason to the human next to the draft so they know why the agent stopped.
identified_risks: Draft-on-failure can mask real bugs if the team only watches send success rates.
A flood of degraded drafts under load could bury the human in review work.
identified_opportunities: Draft-first defaults let the team ship the agent before send reliability is proven.
Degraded drafts double as a labeled dataset of agent near-misses for later tuning.

experts.name: Ilse Marchetti
experts.role: Product operations and inbox triage lead

experts.lens: Evaluates handoffs by whether the conversation visibly continues for the user: ownership labels, status indicators, and a clear return path matter more than internal elegance.

Public pages for Orchid (formerly Zero and Mail0) position it around an AI inbox/agent experience, but public material does not show a concrete, user-visible ownership model for a thread once an agent takes it. If the handoff is expressed only in internal routing state, the user sees a conversation that silently changes hands: replies arrive from a different actor, the status field says something only operators understand, and there is no obvious way to pull the thread back to a human. The former Zero/Mail0 lineage suggests an audience already primed for agent-assisted email, so a clear 'agent has this, here is how to take it back' pattern can be documented and reused across support and triage. Back those with two internal artifacts: a handoff runbook that defines when an agent may take a thread and what it must post at the moment of takeover, and an escalation trigger list (stalled reply, user asks for

insights.insight: The handoff should be visible in the thread itself, as an ownership label plus a plain-language takeover message, so the user never has to infer that an agent now owns the conversation.
insights.supporting_reasoning: From a triage-operations lens, a handoff that lives only in internal state is indistinguishable from a dropped conversation to the person reading the inbox. Orchid's public positioning around an AI inbox makes agent takeover a core moment, and the moment is exactly where users decide whether the product is trustworthy. A visible label and a takeover message cost little and give the user a fixed reference point: they can see the change of hands, and the same label gives support staff a shared anchor when the user replies. The message also forces the agent to state its role, which reduces the ambiguity of a reply arriving from an unfamiliar actor.
implementation_ideas: Add a thread-level ownership label with user-readable values such as 'Handled by agent' and 'Handled by a person', shown wherever the thread appears.
Require the agent to post a short takeover message naming itself and stating that the user can ask for a person at any time.
Show the ownership label in the thread list and in the thread header so the state is visible before the user opens the conversation.
identified_risks: Label values drift into internal jargon that users cannot parse.
The takeover message becomes boilerplate the agent skips under load.
identified_opportunities: The ownership label becomes a reusable trust pattern across every agent-assisted thread.
The takeover message doubles as a template support staff can audit.

insights.insight: The status field must use the same short, user-readable vocabulary internally and externally, or the handoff will look consistent on paper and inconsistent in the inbox.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Status fields fail when operators and users read different words for the same state. In triage operations the temptation is to add internal-only values for routing convenience, and those values leak into what the user sees or diverge from it. Keeping a handful of values that read as plain language, and publishing that exact list to support and triage, means the label the user sees is the label the operator acts on. This is a documentation and discipline problem more than an engineering one, which is why it is cheap to fix early and expensive to unwind later.
implementation_ideas: Define a closed list of user-readable status values, for example 'Open', 'Agent working', 'Waiting on you', and 'Returned to a person'.
Publish the same list in the internal runbook with a one-line definition of when each value is set and cleared.
Add a review step that rejects any new status value that a user could not understand without training.
identified_risks: Internal routing needs push for extra hidden values that then leak into the UI.
Status values go stale if nothing clears them when the thread changes hands.
identified_opportunities: A shared vocabulary shortens triage onboarding and reduces mislabeled threads.
The status list becomes a spec other agent features can reuse.

insights.insight: A one-click return path to a human, backed by an explicit escalation trigger list, is what keeps the handoff from becoming a dead end.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The clearest test of a handoff is whether the conversation visibly continues for the user. An agent that takes a thread and stalls leaves the user with no move except waiting or starting over. A visible 'Return to a person' control gives the user agency, and an escalation trigger list gives the system its own reasons to hand back: a stalled reply, a direct request for a person, a low-confidence answer, or repeated back-and-forth. Pairing the control with triggers means the return path fires even when the user does not know to ask, and preserving the thread history on return means the human picks up mid-conversation instead of restarting it.
implementation_ideas: Add a 'Return to a person' control on every agent-owned thread that reopens it with a human owner and keeps the full history.
Write an escalation trigger list into the runbook covering stalled replies, direct requests for a person, low-confidence answers, and repeated back-and-forth.
Log each return with the trigger that fired so the team can see which triggers do the work and which never fire.
identified_risks: The control invites returns the agent could have handled, adding human load.
Triggers fire too eagerly and thrash ownership between agent and human.
identified_opportunities: Return-path logs become evidence for tuning agent scope.
A visible escape hatch raises user willingness to let an agent take the thread at all.

experts.name: Oskar Nwadike
experts.background: Reviewed OAuth scopes and least-privilege designs for calendar and mail integrations; writes about consent surfaces and what an assistant should be allowed to touch per thread.
experts.lens: Scopes every handoff to explicit per-thread permissions and asks which artifacts prove the agent stayed inside them, including what the user sees and can revoke.

The core risk is scope creep by default: if handing a thread to an agent is implemented as an account-wide OAuth grant or a mailbox-wide token, the agent inherits read/send rights over threads the user never consciously delegated. Explicit consent surfaces (a handoff card listing scopes: read thread, draft, send-as, attach, calendar lookup) create a trust artifact competitors lack. A per-thread grant ledger with a user-facing activity view and one-click revoke gives the team provable least-privilege evidence and gives the user control. Scoping the agent to thread-local context also reduces blast radius and makes the agent's outputs eas
experts.recommendation: Implement thread handoff as an explicit, revocable, per-thread capability grant rather than an account-wide agent token. Concretely: (1) a handoff consent card shown at the moment of delegation, enumerating the exact scopes requested for this thread only (read messages in thread, draft replies, send on user's behalf, read attachments, optional calendar free/busy) with a plain-language 'what the agent can and cannot touch' line; (2) a signed grant record bound to thread ID, grantor, scopes, expiry, and agent version, stored server-side and surfaced in a per-thread 'Agent access' panel; (3) an a

insights.insight: Consent for thread handoff must be a distinct, per-thread surface, not an implicit consequence of enabling the agent on the account.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public descriptions of Orchid/Zero/Mail0 center on the agent acting inside email, but thread-level delegation is a separate consent event from account connection. If the only consent moment is initial OAuth, the user's mental model ('the agent has my mail') never narrows to ('the agent has this thread'). A dedicated handoff card at delegation time creates the record of intent, lets scopes be enumerated in context, and gives the user a decision point before any read or draft occurs. implementation_ideas: Render a handoff card in the thread view listing requested scopes (read thread, draft, send-as, attachments, calendar) with toggles for optional scopes and a default of read+draft only.
Require an explicit confirm action on the card before the agent's first read; show a compact 'Agent has: read, draft on this thread' chip in the thread header afterward.
Record the confirmed scope set in the grant record and display the same set verbatim in the per-thread Agent access panel so consent and state cannot diverge.
identified_risks: Card fatigue if every handoff prompts; users may click through without reading.
Scope toggles that the backend cannot actually enforce become false consent.
Handoff initiated from mobile or a notification may lack room for the full card.
identified_opportunities: A visible consent chip becomes a trust signal in demos and screenshots.
Defaulting to read+draft lowers the decision cost while preserving least privilege.
The card doubles as onboarding for what the agent can do.

insights.insight: The team needs a signed, thread-bound grant record as the primary artifact proving the agent stayed inside its boundary.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An action log alone shows what happened but not what was authorized; without the authorization record you cannot distinguish a permitted send from a scope violation. A grant record binding thread ID, grantor identity, exact scopes, expiry, and agent version makes every subsequent action checkable against a declared boundary. It also makes revocation deterministic: revoke flips the grant state and the enforcement layer denies further actions. This is the artifact that lets the team answer 'prove it' in review, incident response, or a customer security questionnaire, and it is the object the user-facing panel renders.
implementation_ideas: Store grants server-side with fields: grant_id, thread_id, grantor, scope list, created_at, expires_at, agent_version, state (active/revoked/expired); sign or hash-chain the record.
Enforce at the tool-call layer: every agent read/draft/send checks an active grant for that thread and scope before executing, denying with a typed error otherwise.
Expose the grant record read-only in the per-thread Agent access panel and include grant_id in exported audit bundles.
identified_risks: Grant records that are mutable in place lose evidentiary value; edits must be versioned.
Enforcement bugs that check account scope instead of thread grant silently widen the boundary.
Expiry defaults that are too long or absent recreate standing access.
identified_opportunities: Grant records feed security reviews and enterprise procurement answers.
Typed denial errors make enforcement testable.
Short default expiry with renewal keeps grants fresh and intentional.

insights.insight: Revocation and handback must be first-class thread events that preserve the conversation and leave a user-visible trace.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client problem is handing off without dropping the conversation; the mirror problem is taking it back without dropping it. If revoke is buried in settings or silently kills the agent mid-draft, the user loses work and trust. Revocation should invalidate the grant immediately, have the agent post a short handback summary (what it read, drafted, sent, and what remains open) into the thread, and mark the thread human-owned. The handback summary plus the frozen action log are the artifacts showing the agent stopped exactly at revoke. This closes the loop on the consent surface: grant, act, revoke, prove.
implementation_ideas: Put a Revoke control in the thread header chip and the Agent access panel; on click, invalidate the grant, halt in-flight tool calls, and post an agent-authored handback summary to the thread.
Freeze the action log at revoke with a terminal 'revoked by user at timestamp' entry and keep it visible in the panel.
Offer a one-step 'renew grant' from the same panel that reuses the prior scope set with a fresh expiry and a new consent confirm.
identified_risks: In-flight sends at revoke time may complete after the user expects a stop; needs a clear rule (finish current call vs abort).
Handback summaries could leak content the user thought was discarded.
Renew flows may become rubber-stamped and erode the consent moment.
identified_opportunities: Clean handback makes users more willing to delegate again.
Frozen logs give a defensible end-state for disputes.
Renew-with-prior-scopes reduces friction without widening rights.
