insights.supporting_reasoning: Public descriptions of Orchid frame the product around agents acting in the inbox, but nothing public states how two actors touching one thread are serialized. If ownership is a boolean, a human edit during an agent run and an agent commit can both land, and whichever writes last wins with no record of the conflict. Treating the handoff as a lease with an expected revision makes the conflict explicit: the loser gets a stale-revision rejection and must rebase onto the committed thread. This is the same discipline as optimistic concurrency in durable task queues, applied to conversation state, and it is what makes the transition reversible rather than destructive.
implementation_ideas: Define a thread-state record with revision counter, current owner, lease id, and lease expiry; every write carries the expected revision.
On stale-revision rejection, force the agent to re-read the committed thread and re-plan before retrying, rather than retrying blindly.
Expose lease state in the UI so a human sees the agent holds the thread and can revoke the lease explicitly.
identified_risks: Lease expiry tuning is guesswork without public latency data; too short causes churn, too long blocks humans.
Rebase logic on the agent side can loop if the human keeps editing during the retry window.
identified_opportunities: Deterministic conflict resolution becomes a defensible reliability claim the public pages do not make.
The lease record is reusable for bot-to-bot handoffs, not just human-to-bot.

insights.insight: Every handoff must be an append-only event so a stalled agent run is observable and resumable from the last committed state, not restarted from scratch or abandoned mid-thread.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The failure mode that drops conversations is a stall with no record: the agent stops, the thread sits in an ambiguous owner state, and the human cannot tell whether the agent is thinking, dead, or done. An append-only event log (requested, granted, stalled, resumed, returned, revoked) turns the stall into a first-class state with a timestamp and a recovery path. Because the log is append-only and the thread revision is monotonic, a resume can reconstruct exactly what the agent had committed and what it had not, so continuity survives the stall. This also gives an audit trail for the human-edit-mid-run case, since the edit and the agent's prior commits are both ordered in the log.
implementation_ideas: Emit a handoff event on every transition with actor, timestamp, prior and new revision, and reason code.
Add a stall detector that fires on lease expiry or heartbeat miss and writes a stalled event, then notifies the human owner.
Implement resume as replay from the last committed revision plus the event log, so the agent re-enters at a known point.
identified_risks: Event log growth per thread needs a compaction or snapshot strategy that public pages give no guidance on.
Heartbeat-based stall detection can false-positive on slow model calls and trigger unnecessary resumes.
identified_opportunities: The event log doubles as the audit artifact for reversibility and compliance questions.
Stall-and-resume handling is a visible reliability story for an agentic inbox.

insights.insight: The team's first artifacts should be the handoff contract and its state schema, versioned alongside the thread, because an unversioned handoff silently breaks when either the agent or the human side changes.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A handoff spans two actors that evolve independently: the agent's planning loop and the human's client. If the contract is implicit, a change on one side (a new field, a different commit order) breaks the other with no signal, and the conversation drops in a way that looks like a bug rather than a version mismatch. Versioning the contract and the thread-state schema makes the break explicit and lets the system reject or migrate an incompatible actor. This is the same reason durable state machines version their transition tables: reversibility depends on being able to identify which contract a given run was operating under.
implementation_ideas: Version the handoff contract and thread-state schema, and stamp each run with the contract version it acquired the lease under.
Reject or migrate writes from an actor on a stale contract version at the lease boundary, with a clear reason code.
Keep a short migration note per contract version so the team can trace which runs used which semantics.
identified_risks: Versioning adds friction to fast iteration and can stall small changes behind migration work.
Public pages give no signal on Orchid's release cadence, so version churn assumptions are unverified.
identified_opportunities: A versioned contract makes the orchestration layer safe to change without dropping live threads.
It creates a documented interface other agent builders could target.

experts.name: Noor Haddad
experts.background: Worked on IMAP/SMTP sync engines and open-source mail clients, including thread-ID stability, label propagation, and draft reconciliation across devices. Familiar with MCP-style tool surfaces for thread retrieval and send/draft actions.
experts.lens: Reads the problem through the mail data model: thread identity, message ordering, label semantics, and how a draft stays a draft across sync boundaries without forking the conversation.
experts.risks: Thread handoff to an agent is fundamentally a mail-data-model problem: if the agent operates on a message or a client-side thread guess rather than a stable thread identity, the conversation forks. Publicly visible risk areas: (1) Thread identity is not portable — RFC 5322 References/In-Reply-To and provider thread IDs (Gmail threadId, Graph conversationId) disagree, and Orchid's public positioning around an AI-native mail client implies server-side thread objects whose stability across IMAP/SMTP, Gmail API, and Graph is unproven from public pages. (2) Draft semantics: an agent-authored reply
experts.opportunities: The same model gives Orchid a defensible design: make the handoff artifact a thread-scoped, versioned envelope rather than a message. Opportunities: (1) A canonical thread object with a stable internal thread ID plus a mapping table to provider IDs lets the agent work provider-agnostically and lets the client re-render without forking. (2) Draft-as-artifact with a client-generated draft UUID carried in a custom header (e.g. X-Orchid-Draft-Id) makes reconciliation deterministic across devices and lets the agent revise its own draft idempotently. (3) Namespaced agent labels (agent/<name>/<state>
experts.recommendation: Hand off a thread-scoped envelope, not a message, and make draft-only the default action. Concretely: the client resolves the thread to a canonical internal thread ID, snapshots the ordered message-ID set with a watermark, and passes an envelope {thread_id, provider_thread_ref, message_ids[], watermark, allowed_actions:[draft], agent_label_namespace, expiry, draft_uuid}. The agent returns artifacts keyed by draft_uuid and thread_id; the sync engine reconciles drafts by UUID before APPEND and treats a missing UUID as a new draft. Require an explicit handback event that clears the agent label na

insights.insight: Thread identity must be an Orchid-owned canonical ID with a provider mapping, because provider thread IDs and RFC 5322 headers are not interchangeable and an agent keyed to either will fork conversations.
insights.supporting_reasoning: IMAP has no thread ID at all; threading is reconstructed from References/In-Reply-To and Subject, and clients differ in normalization. Gmail exposes threadId and Graph exposes conversationId, but these are provider-scoped and not stable across a migration or a re-sync. If the agent is handed a message-ID or a provider thread ref, any provider change or header rewrite (subject prefix stripping, broken References from a third-party sender) splits the agent's view from the user's view, and the agent's draft lands in a different thread than the one the user opened. A canonical internal ID plus a mapping table keeps the agent provider-agnostic and lets the client re-render the same thread after sync. This is the mail-data-model equivalent of not keying on a mutable field.
implementation_ideas: Define an internal thread_id assigned at first observation, with a mapping table (thread_id, provider, provider_thread_ref, first_seen, last_verified) and a re-resolution job that repairs mappings when provider refs change.
Hand the agent only thread_id plus an ordered message-ID set; never expose raw provider thread refs in the agent contract.
Add a fork detector that flags when an inbound message's References resolve to a different thread_id than the envelope's, and route it to human review instead of auto-drafting.
identified_risks: Mapping table drift after provider migration or mailbox re-sync produces orphaned thread_ids.
Third-party senders with broken References create false fork alerts and stall the agent.
identified_opportunities: Provider-agnostic agent contract eases adding IMAP, Gmail, and Graph backends.
Stable thread_id enables reliable per-thread audit logs and evals.

insights.insight: A draft must be a first-class artifact with a client-generated UUID, because IMAP draft reconciliation is append/expunge-based and an agent that revises drafts without an identity will duplicate or fork them across devices.
insights.supporting_reasoning: IMAP has no draft identity: a draft is a message in the Drafts folder, and updates are APPEND plus EXPUNGE of the old copy. Two devices (or a device and an agent) revising concurrently each APPEND, and the server keeps both; the user then sees two drafts in one thread. Gmail and Graph have draft IDs but they are provider-scoped and do not survive a move to IMAP. Carrying a client-generated draft UUID in a custom header makes reconciliation deterministic: the sync engine matches on UUID before APPEND, treats a missing UUID as a new draft, and collapses revisions to the latest by timestamp. This also lets the agent revise idempotently on retry without creating a second draft, and it keeps the draft inside the thread rather than as a detached message.
implementation_ideas: Stamp every agent draft with X-Orchid-Draft-Id (UUIDv4) and X-Orchid-Thread-Id; reconcile by UUID in the sync engine before any APPEND.
Implement a draft state machine (created → revised → sent | discarded) where only one state transition per UUID is accepted and stale revisions are dropped by timestamp.
Run a two-device concurrency test: agent revises while a second client edits, and assert exactly one draft survives in the thread.
identified_risks: Custom headers may be stripped by some relays or providers, breaking UUID matching.
Timestamp-based stale-revision dropping can discard a legitimate later edit if clocks skew.
identified_opportunities: Idempotent draft revision makes agent retries safe.
Draft UUIDs give a clean audit trail of agent revisions per thread.

insights.insight: Agent state needs a namespaced label scheme and an explicit handback event, because otherwise agent labels collide with user labels and the agent stays subscribed to the thread indefinitely.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Labels are user-meaningful in IMAP (folders) and Gmail (labels), and an agent writing bare labels like "handled" or "todo" collides with user vocabulary and is hard to reverse. A namespace such as agent/<name>/<state> keeps agent state separable, reversible, and visible without polluting user labels. Separately, "take the thread" has no natural end: without an expiry and a handback event that clears the namespace and closes the envelope, the agent keeps receiving messages and the user cannot tell who owns the thread. An explicit handback (plus envelope expiry) makes ownership legible and gives the sync engine a clean point to stop routing messages to the agent.
implementation_ideas: Adopt agent/<name>/<state> labels (e.g. agent/triage/active, agent/triage/done) and render them in a separate UI group from user labels.
Define a handback event that clears the agent label namespace, expires the envelope, and writes a closing entry to the per-thread event log.
Add an envelope expiry (message count or wall-clock) after which the agent is auto-handed-back with a notification to the user.
identified_risks: Folder-based IMAP backends cannot express multi-label state and need a mapping to folders.
Auto-expiry can hand back mid-task and leave a half-finished draft.
identified_opportunities: Namespaced labels make agent state reversible and auditable.
Explicit handback improves user trust and bounds agent cost.

experts.name: Beatrix Okonjo
experts.background: Studies approval-first assistant interfaces, measuring where users lose trust when automation acts without consent. Has run diary studies on inbox triage tools and designed visible ownership indicators for shared queues.
experts.lens: Insists the thread must always show who owns it and what the agent is doing; evaluates every artifact against whether a user can see, interrupt, and resume the agent without ambiguity.
experts.risks: From a consent-and-ownership lens, the biggest risk is that 'handing a thread to an agent' is described as a transfer of work rather than a visible, reversible state change. If the thread does not carry a persistent owner badge (human vs. agent, named agent, acting-on-behalf-of) and a plain-language statement of what the agent will do next, users will experience silent automation and lose trust the first time the agent sends something they did not expect. A second risk is interruptibility theater: a Stop button that pauses generation but leaves queued sends, scheduled follow-ups, or draft muta
experts.opportunities: The handoff is a chance to make ownership a first-class, visible object rather than an inference. A thread header that always answers 'who owns this right now, and what are they doing' is a differentiator in a category where most assistants hide their state. Because the client controls the whole surface, the team can design a handoff ritual: an explicit, scoped grant (this thread, these actions, until this condition) that is as easy to revoke as to give. Interruption can be designed as a first-class verb with a defined landing state, so 'take it back' always resolves to a clear human-owned thr
experts.recommendation: Treat the handoff as a visible, scoped, revocable state change, and make the thread's ownership indicator the primary artifact the team designs first. Concretely: define a small ownership state machine (human-owned, agent-proposed, agent-acting, paused-by-human, returned-to-human, done) where every transition is user-visible in the thread and every agent transition has an explicit grant scope. Build the thread header badge and the handoff card before building agent capability, so capability is constrained by legibility. Pair it with an interruption spec that guarantees a defined landing state

insights.insight: Ownership must be a persistent, visible thread property, not a mode the user has to remember.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In approval-first interfaces, trust collapses at the moment a user discovers automation they did not know was running. A mode toggle in settings is invisible during reading; a badge in the thread header is not. Because a thread can have multiple humans (sender, CCs, queue members) plus an agent, the indicator must name the current owner and the agent's acting-on-behalf-of human, otherwise 'the agent has it' is ambiguous about who is accountable. The state must also be readable at a glance by someone who just opened the thread, which rules out subtle iconography alone. This is a design claim grounded in how visibility supports interruptibility, not a measured result.
implementation_ideas: Thread header ownership badge with three states rendered in words plus icon: 'You own this', 'Orchid agent acting for you', 'Paused, you own this', always naming the human on whose behalf the agent acts.
A handoff card inserted at the point in the thread where the agent takes over, stating scope ('draft replies only', 'until Friday', 'this thread only') and offering Revoke inline.
A per-thread activity strip showing the agent's current step in plain language ('reading thread', 'drafting reply', 'waiting for your approval') that persists while the agent is active.
identified_risks: Badge clutter in threads with many participants; the indicator may compete with sender identity and be misread.
Users may assume the badge is decorative if it never changes state visibly during normal use.
Naming an acting-on-behalf-of human can misattribute ownership in shared queues where the queue, not a person, is the real owner.
identified_opportunities: The ownership badge becomes a reusable primitive for teammate handoffs and shared queues, not just agent handoffs.
Visible state gives the team a natural place to hang instrumentation and later diary-study prompts.
A clear badge reduces support burden by answering 'who did this' inside the thread.

insights.insight: Interruption must land in a defined state; a Stop button that only halts generation is worse than none.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Users judge interruptibility by consequences, not by the presence of a control. If pressing Stop leaves a queued send, a scheduled follow-up, or a half-mutated draft, the user learns that stopping does not stop and will either over-supervise or disengage. The design therefore needs an explicit landing state: agent halts, ownership returns to a named human, and any partial work is preserved as a clearly labeled draft or note rather than silently discarded or silently sent. Preserving partial work matters because discarding it punishes the user for interrupting. Requiring the human to re-grant before the agent resumes prevents the agent from quietly re-taking the thread after a pause. This is a state-machine argument, testable in a diary study but not yet measured here.
implementation_ideas: A single Interrupt control available wherever the agent is active, which transitions the thread to 'Paused, you own this' and freezes all queued agent actions, not just the current one.
On interrupt, convert the agent's in-progress output into a labeled draft or thread note ('Agent draft, paused') that the human can edit, send, or discard.
A resume gate: the agent cannot act again until the human presses 'Hand back to agent', which re-shows the scope before confirming.
identified_risks: Users may interrupt reflexively and generate draft clutter that itself becomes a triage problem.
Freezing queued actions can strand time-sensitive sends the user expected to go out.
If the paused draft is mistaken for a sent message, users may believe a reply went out when it did not.
identified_opportunities: Defined landing states make interruption measurable (time-to-interrupt, resume rate) for later study.
Preserved partial work turns interruption into a collaboration rather than a reset.
A resume gate creates a natural checkpoint for scope review.

insights.insight: The team needs handoff artifacts that encode consent and audit, not just flow diagrams.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A flow diagram shows where the agent goes; it does not show what the user consented to or how they reconstruct events later. Because the client problem is specifically about not dropping the conversation, the artifacts must make the handoff event, its scope, and every interruption and resume visible and durable in the thread. That means a state machine with named states and allowed transitions, a handoff card spec, an interruption/resume spec, and an event log rendered in-thread. These artifacts also constrain engineering: if a proposed agent capability cannot be expressed as a visible transition with a grant scope, it is not ready. The audit trail matters most after a surprise, which is precisely when users decide whether to trust the product again. This is a design-process claim from prior diary-study practice, not a benchmarked outcome.
implementation_ideas: A one-page ownership state machine listing states, allowed transitions, who may trigger each, and the visible artifact each transition produces.
A handoff card spec covering required fields: scope of actions, expiry condition, acting-on-behalf-of human, and revoke affordance.
An in-thread event log entry for each transition ('Agent took thread, drafts only', 'You paused the agent', 'You handed back, scope re-confirmed') that is collapsible but never deleted.
identified_risks: Artifact overhead can slow the team and produce specs that drift from the shipped interface.
An in-thread event log may feel like noise to recipients who are not the owner.
State machines designed without engineering input can encode transitions the system cannot actually enforce.
identified_opportunities: Artifacts double as QA checklists and onboarding material for new engineers and designers.
The event log supports later diary-study reconstruction without extra instrumentation.
Scope fields create a reusable consent pattern for future agent capabilities.

experts.name: Emil Sarkisian
experts.background: Designed permission scopes and approval workflows for assistant products operating inside third-party apps, including draft-only modes and per-action consent. Has audited handoff flows for privilege escalation between agents.
experts.lens: Maps each handoff to explicit permissions and an approval gate; asks which actions the agent may take autonomously versus which must return to the human, and how scope is narrowed on return.
experts.risks: Public pages for Orchid (orchid.ai, formerly Zero/Mail0) do not document a formal permission-scope model, per-action consent UI, or an approval-gate contract for agent handoff, so any handoff design must be inferred from product positioning rather than confirmed capability. The core risk is privilege escalation across the handoff: if the agent inherits the human's full mailbox scope (read, send, label, archive, delete, external-forward) at the moment of handoff, a draft-only or review-first posture collapses silently and the agent can send or mutate state the human never approved. A second ris
experts.opportunities: A well-designed handoff is a differentiator for an email product: email is a high-stakes, externally visible channel where draft-only and per-action consent are credible trust features. Orchid can make the handoff itself the permission boundary: a scoped, time-boxed, thread-local grant that narrows on return rather than a global agent mode. The artifacts the team needs are also an opportunity to standardize: a handoff contract (who holds the thread, what scopes, expiry), a scope-narrowing matrix for return, an approval-gate spec distinguishing autonomous actions from human-gated ones, and an a
experts.recommendation: Implement handoff as an explicit, thread-local, time-boxed capability grant with a mandatory approval gate on outbound send, and never transfer the human's ambient mailbox scope. Concretely: the human initiates handoff from the thread, the system mints a scoped token limited to that thread (read thread, draft reply, apply labels, propose archive) with an expiry and a named human owner; the agent operates in draft-only mode by default; any send, external forward, or destructive action returns to the human as an approval request inside the thread; on return, scopes narrow automatically to read-p

insights.insight: The handoff, not the agent mode, should be the unit of permission: grant thread-local, time-boxed scopes at handoff and narrow them on return, rather than toggling a global agent mode.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Email agents fail trust in two directions: too little scope and they cannot act, too much and they send unapproved mail. A global mode grants ambient mailbox rights that persist after the thread is done, which is exactly where privilege escalation hides. Making the handoff the grant boundary means every capability is tied to a specific thread, a specific human owner, and an expiry, so the blast radius is one conversation. Narrowing on return is the mirror requirement: when the agent hands back, residual send or rule-creation rights must be revoked by default and re-granted explicitly, not carried forward. This also makes the approval gate auditable, because each scope has a mint time, an owner, and a revocation event.
implementation_ideas: Define a handoff contract object with fields: thread_id, granting_human, granted_scopes[], expiry, revocation_trigger, and approving_principal; mint it at handoff and store it with the thread.
Default the grant to draft-only (read thread, create draft, apply labels) and require a separate explicit grant for send, external forward, and delete.
On return, run an automatic scope-narrowing step that revokes send and rule-creation rights, logs the revocation, and leaves only read-plus-draft for the human.
identified_risks: Expiry that fires mid-conversation can strand a thread with no owner if the human is away; needs a grace state that notifies the owner rather than silently dropping scope.
Scope tokens stored per thread add state to manage and can drift from actual agent behavior if enforcement is advisory rather than checked at action time.
identified_opportunities: A visible scope badge on the thread (who holds it, what it may do, when it expires) turns an internal control into a user-facing trust signal.
Thread-local grants make the audit log trivially scoped and reviewable per conversation.

insights.insight: Outbound send is the one action that must always return to the human; everything reversible can be autonomous, and the approval gate should live inside the thread so continuity is preserved.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client problem is handing off without dropping the conversation, which tempts a design where the agent replies directly. But send is externally visible and hard to retract, so it is the natural gate. Reversible actions (drafting, labeling, summarizing, proposing archive) can run autonomously because the human can undo them cheaply. Placing the approval request in-thread, as a draft the human approves or edits, keeps the conversation live and keeps the human as sender of record, so no commitment is made without a human. This also gives a clean autonomous-versus-gated matrix: autonomy is a function of reversibility and external visibility, not of agent confidence.
implementation_ideas: Build an action matrix classifying each agent action as autonomous (draft, label, summarize, propose archive) or gated (send, external forward, delete, create standing rule), enforced at action time.
Render gated actions as an in-thread approval card showing the proposed draft, the scopes used, and approve/edit/reject controls, with the human as sender of record.
Log every autonomous action with its scope token so the human can review what the agent did without a gate.
identified_risks: Approval fatigue: if the agent drafts many replies, the human may rubber-stamp without reading, weakening the gate.
An in-thread approval card can be mistaken for a sent message by recipients or by the human, causing duplicate sends.
identified_opportunities: Approval cards double as a training and trust surface, showing exactly what the agent would do before it does it.
The reversibility rule generalizes to other channels (calendar, tasks) if Orchid expands beyond email.

insights.insight: The return path is where privilege escalation actually happens, so the team needs an explicit scope-narrowing and handback spec, not just a handoff spec.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Most handoff designs specify what the agent gets and stop there. But the dangerous moment is return: the agent may keep send rights, standing rules, or scheduled follow-ups that the human assumes ended, and the human resumes with stale assumptions about what the agent can still do. Auditing handoff flows shows escalation usually enters on the way back, not the way out. A handback spec must define what narrows automatically, what is revoked, what the human must re-grant, and how the thread ownership transfers back with full context so nothing is dropped. Without it, the handoff contract is one-directional and the audit log has no closing event.
implementation_ideas: Write a handback spec enumerating each scope with a return behavior: auto-revoke (send, delete, rule creation), narrow-to-read (thread access), and retain-with-notice (draft history).
Require an explicit handback event that transfers thread ownership to the named human, restores their full context, and writes a closing audit entry.
Surface a post-return summary to the human listing what the agent did, what scopes were revoked, and anything still pending their approval.
identified_risks: Auto-revocation on return can cancel a scheduled follow-up the human expected the agent to complete; needs a pending-items carry-over rule.
If handback is implicit (agent goes idle) rather than an explicit event, revocation may never fire and scopes leak.
identified_opportunities: An explicit handback event with a summary is a natural review checkpoint and a differentiator versus agents that just go quiet.
The narrowing matrix becomes a reusable artifact for any future agent surface.

experts.name: Junia Ferreira-Lund
experts.background: Built sync and callback layers connecting assistants to external stacks, including status webhooks and conflict resolution when a human and an agent edit the same object. Has shipped return-to-owner flows for delegated tasks.
experts.lens: Focuses on the sync and return path: how agent status propagates back to the thread, how conflicts resolve, and how control visibly returns to the human so the conversation is never orphaned.
experts.risks: Public pages for Orchid (orchid.ai, formerly Zero/Mail0) describe an AI email client but, from what is publicly visible, do not document a thread-handoff or return-path contract. The core risk is that the team builds an agent 'take thread' action as a one-way door: the agent's status never propagates back to the thread, the human loses the thread's state, and the conversation is orphaned. Secondary risks: conflict resolution when a human and agent edit the same draft or reply is unspecified, so last-write-wins silently clobbers human edits; the return-to-owner path is invisible, so humans cann
experts.opportunities: A visible, well-specified return path is a differentiator: if Orchid makes agent status and control return legible in the thread, it avoids the orphaned-conversation failure mode common to agent handoffs. The handoff moment is also a natural place to define artifacts the team can build against: an ownership/lease record, a status event stream, and a conflict-resolution log. Getting this right early means the same contract can cover delegated tasks beyond email (follow-ups, scheduling) and gives the team a testable spec instead of demo-driven guesswork.
experts.recommendation: Define the handoff as a reversible lease, not a transfer. Before any agent takes a thread, Orchid should write an explicit ownership record (who holds the thread, since when, under what scope) and emit status events back into the thread itself so the human always sees the agent's state. Control returns to the human on completion, on a timeout, or on human edit, with conflicts resolved by a stated rule (e.g., human edit wins and pauses the agent) and logged. The team's first artifacts should be: (1) the ownership/lease schema, (2) the status-event contract rendered in-thread, and (3) the confli

insights.insight: Agent status must propagate back into the thread as visible events, not sit in a separate agent dashboard.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The failure mode in delegated email is the orphaned thread: the human hands off, the agent works invisibly, and the human cannot tell if it is running, stuck, or finished. If status lives only in an agent console, the thread itself goes stale and the human's mental model diverges from reality. Emitting status events (taken, working, needs-input, returned) into the thread keeps the conversation self-describing and makes the return path observable. This is inference from the public product framing of an AI email client, not a documented Orchid behavior.
implementation_ideas: Define a status-event schema (event type, actor, timestamp, thread id, reason) and render each event as an in-thread system line.
Add a 'needs input' event that pauses the agent and surfaces a prompt in the thread rather than in a side panel.
Emit a terminal 'returned to owner' event on every exit path, including timeout and error, so no thread ends silently.
identified_risks: Status-event noise clutters the thread if every internal step is emitted.
Event rendering may leak agent internals the human does not need.
identified_opportunities: Status events double as an audit trail for who held the thread and when.
A visible return event builds trust and makes handoff reversible in the human's eyes.

insights.insight: Handoff should be a scoped, expiring lease with an explicit return-to-owner trigger, not a permanent transfer.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A permanent transfer means the human must remember to reclaim the thread, and forgotten threads orphan. A lease with a scope (which actions the agent may take) and an expiry forces a defined return path: on completion, on timeout, or on human intervention. The lease record also gives conflict resolution something to key on, since ownership is explicit rather than assumed. This mirrors return-to-owner flows for delegated tasks and is a design inference for Orchid, not a confirmed feature.
implementation_ideas: Store an ownership record with holder, scope, start time, and expiry; require it before the agent can act.
Auto-return control to the human on lease expiry and emit the return event in-thread.
Let a human reclaim the thread at any time with one action that revokes the lease and pauses the agent.
identified_risks: Too-short leases cause the agent to drop mid-task; too-long leases delay human reclaim.
Scope enforcement may be incomplete and let the agent act outside its lease.
identified_opportunities: Lease expiry bounds the blast radius of a stuck agent.
Explicit scope makes agent permissions auditable per thread.

insights.insight: Concurrent human and agent edits need a stated conflict rule and a log, or the return path silently clobbers human work.
insights.supporting_reasoning: When a human and an agent edit the same draft or reply, last-write-wins loses whichever edit landed first, and the human may not notice. A stated rule (human edit wins and pauses the agent; agent proposes rather than overwrites) plus a conflict log makes resolution predictable and reviewable. Without it, the return path is technically present but the human's control is not real. This is a general sync-layer inference applied to Orchid's public framing.
implementation_ideas: Adopt a rule that a human edit pauses the agent and marks the agent's pending change as a proposal.
Write each conflict to a log (thread id, both versions, resolution, timestamp) retrievable from the thread.
Show a diff or proposal marker in-thread when the agent's change was superseded, so the human sees what was dropped.
identified_risks: Pausing on every human keystroke could thrash the agent.

debate.statement: I'll agree with Tobias Lindqvist, because the return path is where this design actually lives or dies, and his 'hand it over by ID, not by copy' is the right spine. Concretely, the handoff manifest should carry a lease TTL and a single-writer token, and the return-path events (started, draft-ready, sent, failed, returned) should be keyed on (thread_id, lease_id, idempotency_key) so a retried or crashed agent run converges to one terminal state instead of double-drafting or double-sending. top5.title: Ship a versioned Thread Handoff Contract with CAS-guarded state machine as the first artifact
top5.detail: Define a single versioned thread-state record before any agent UX: immutable thread_id, append-only event log with content hashes, owner field, approval gate, agent lease with TTL, and a monotonically increasing state version. The state machine (unassigned -> offered -> agent-held -> awaiting-approval -> returned/escalated -> closed) has every transition idempotent, logged, and guarded by compare-and-swap on the state version. Ship the schema, transition table, and idempotency keys first, with a conformance test. The debate converged on this ordering: Priya's contract-first spine was endorsed by Marcus, Dana, Tobias, Lena, Rafael, Kwame, and Calder, with amendments that the CAS must be on the log head (Lena, Calder, Priya R2) and that 'agent-held' must split into agent-acting and agent-blocked-needs-human (Marcus R2).
top5.rationale: Every panelist who engaged the ordering agreed the contract must precede agent behavior; the only disputes were about field-level shape, which the conformance test can absorb. Without CAS on a durable log head, a human edit mid-run silently overwrites the agent's work.

State vocabulary too backend-flavored for the sender-facing UI (Ingrid, Ilse).
CAS on a scalar version goes stale on concurrent human edits unless pinned to the log head (Lena, Calder).

Build the conformance test and fixture threads before any runtime code.

top5.title: Make the return path a lease with TTL owned by the sync engine, keyed by thread ID
top5.detail: Hand the thread over by ID, not by copy. The client passes a stable thread ID plus a handoff manifest (owner, scope, lease_id, TTL, single-writer token, allowed actions); the agent acts only against that ID and emits return-path events (started, draft-ready, sent, failed, returned) keyed by (thread_id, lease_id, idempotency key). The client reconciles by re-fetching the thread by ID and diffing, then renders owner state and any draft for human review before send. The lease is owned by the sync engine, not the agent runtime, because the runtime is the component we cannot trust to release it. Tobias's return-path spine was endorsed by Junia, who sharpened it into a lease with expiry and a single-writer token.
top5.rationale: The return leg is where the design lives or dies; a thread object with a stable ID is necessary but not sufficient if the client has no defined way to learn what happened. Lease expiry plus single-writer token resolves the two-writer conflict that a bare boolean cannot.

Median time from draft-ready to human review

Specify the return-path event schema keyed by thread_id and lease_id.
Move lease ownership into the sync engine and add a forced-expiry path.

dissenters.why: Wants the lease to live on the versioned thread record with CAS on the log head, not as a parallel structure with its own head to guard.

dissenters.name: Wren Takahashi

top5.title: Bind approval to a revision hash inside a frozen thread envelope; draft-only by default
top5.detail: The agent receives a frozen thread envelope (participants, ordered message-ID set with watermark, attachments, labels, human's stated intent) and may only produce draft revisions inside it. Nothing leaves draft state until a human approves a specific revision; approval binds to that revision hash, and the approved revision converts to a send in the same thread with context intact. Ship the four artifacts (envelope, revision, approval record, send receipt) before any autonomy beyond drafting. Dana's approval binding was endorsed by Oskar, who sharpened it to a revision hash so a stale draft cannot be approved after the thread moved, and by Noor's envelope-over-message, draft-only-default position.
top5.rationale: An approval gate field without a revision binding leaves open what exactly the human approved; a stale draft approved after a human edit is the classic silent failure. Draft-only default keeps the human as the only path to send.

Revision hash binding is bypassed by a runtime that sends directly.
Attachment handling in the envelope leaks scope beyond the thread.

Drafts sent without a matching approval record
Envelope-to-send context diffs caught at review

Enforce revision-hash binding at the send boundary.
Add a stale-revision rejection test to the fixture set.

dissenters.name: Dana Kessler
dissenters.why: Counters that the badge is a rendering of the owner field already on the envelope, so envelope-first does not build capability ahead of legibility.

top5.title: Mint a thread-local, time-boxed capability grant with a mandatory approval gate on send
top5.detail: Implement handoff as an explicit, revocable, per-thread capability grant rather than an account-wide agent token. The human initiates handoff from inside the thread; the system mints a signed grant record bound to thread ID, grantor, scopes (read thread, draft reply, apply labels, propose archive), expiry, and agent version, stored server-side and surfaced in a per-thread 'Agent access' panel with a plain-language what-the-agent-can-and-cannot-touch line. Any send, external forward, or destructive action returns to the human as an approval request inside the thread; on return, scopes narrow automatically to read-only. Never transfer the human's ambient mailbox scope. Emil's trust boundary was endorsed by Oskar, who added the revision-hash binding on the gate.
top5.rationale: Ambient mailbox scope is the boundary most likely to be quietly violated by an account-wide token. Thread-local, expiring grants with a named human owner keep blast radius to one conversation and make revocation trivial.
risks: Grant surface outruns documented Orchid capabilities (Mira, Amara).
Consent card becomes a rubber stamp users click through.
Scope narrowing on return is skipped, leaving the agent read access after handback.
metrics: Grants minted per thread versus account-wide tokens issued
Approval requests raised before outbound send
next_steps: Write the signed grant record schema with scopes, expiry, and agent version.
Build the consent card and per-thread Agent access panel.
Enforce automatic scope narrowing on return-to-human.

dissenters.name: Mira Okonkwo
dissenters.why: Warns the grant surface exceeds the three publicly supported primitives and should be tagged ASSUMED with an owner until Orchid confirms it.

dissenters.name: Amara Sotelo
dissenters.why: Treats any capability not found in public sources as unverified; the consent card presumes a permissions surface the public record does not document.

top5.title: Render ownership state in the thread header and log every transition to an append-only audit trail
top5.detail: Model agent takeover as an explicit, visible ownership state transition, not a background action. Ship an owner field with enumerated states (human-owned, agent-proposed, agent-acting, agent-blocked-needs-human, returned) rendered in the thread header, a handoff event record capturing who handed off, to which agent, why, and the named human return owner, and a mandatory escalation contract defining when the agent must flip to agent-blocked-needs-human and notify the return owner. top5.rationale: A background takeover is indistinguishable from a bug the moment the human's mental model diverges from the agent's. Splitting agent-held into agent-acting and agent-blocked-needs-human is the specific fix for a blocked agent that still reads as held.
risks: Header badge drifts from the underlying owner field if not rendered from it.
Escalation contract under-specified, so blocked agents sit silently.
Audit log grows without a retention policy.
metrics: Time in agent-blocked-needs-human before human action
Handoffs with a named human return owner recorded
State transitions with a matching audit entry
next_steps: Render the header badge directly from the contract's owner field.
Write the escalation contract with explicit blocked-state triggers.
Add the append-only audit entry to every transition handler.

skills.name: thread-handoff-contract
skills.description: Defines and validates a versioned Thread Handoff Contract (state machine, event log, lease, approval gate) that lets an email client hand a thread to an agent by ID without dropping the conversation. Use when designing or reviewing the handoff data model, state transitions, or the CAS-guarded state record before any agent UX is built.
skills.instructions:
# Thread Handoff Contract

## Overview
Produce a single versioned thread-state record and its state machine so a thread can be handed to an agent by ID (not by copy) and returned safely. The record is the first artifact: immutable `thread_id`, append-only event log with content hashes, `owner` field, approval gate, agent lease with TTL, and a monotonically increasing `state_version` guarded by compare-and-swap (CAS).

## When to use
- Before building any agent takeover UX.
- When defining or reviewing the thread state machine, event log, or lease semantics.
- When a handoff or return bug suggests the state model is underspecified.

## Inputs
- Current thread/message data model (IDs, message-ID set, labels, participants).
- Sync engine capabilities (event emission, lease ownership).
- Product decisions on allowed actions and approval levels.

## Steps
1. Draft the record schema from `schema.json`; keep `thread_id` immutable and add `state_version` starting at 1.
2. Encode the state machine: `unassigned -> offered -> agent-held -> awaiting-approval -> returned` (plus `agent-blocked-needs-human`, `failed`, `revoked`). Reject illegal transitions.
3. Make every transition append an event with `(thread_id, state_version, actor, action, content_hash, timestamp)`; never mutate history.
4. Require CAS on `state_version` for every write; on mismatch, reload and retry or surface a conflict.
5. Attach the agent lease: `lease_id`, `ttl_seconds`, single-writer token; expire lease on TTL and revert to `agent-blocked-needs-human`.
6. Add the approval gate: `awaiting-approval` blocks send until a human approves a specific revision hash.
7. Validate a sample thread against `schema.json` and run the illegal-transition cases.

## Output format
- The JSON schema (from `schema.json`, adapted).
- A transition table listing from-state, to-state, actor, guard, and emitted event.
- A short list of CAS conflict and lease-expiry handling rules.

## Guardrails
- Hand off by ID, never by copy.
- No state write without CAS and an appended event.
- No send from `agent-held`; only from an approved revision in `awaiting-approval`.
- Keep the event log append-only; content hashes, not full bodies, in events.

## Example
Thread `t_123` at `state_version` 4, owner `human`. Human offers it: CAS 4->5, event `offered`, lease minted (TTL 900s). Agent accepts: CAS 5->6, state `agent-held`. Agent emits `draft-ready` with revision hash; state `awaiting-approval`. Human approves hash; send allowed. See `schema.json`.

skills.instructions:
# Lease Return Path

## Overview
Hand a thread to an agent by ID with a handoff manifest (owner, scope, lease_id, TTL, single-writer token, allowed actions). The agent acts only against that ID and emits return-path events keyed by `(thread_id, lease_id)`. The sync engine owns the lease and reclaims the thread on TTL expiry or failure.

## When to use
- When implementing the handoff/return transport between client, sync engine, and agent.
- When defining the manifest, lease lifecycle, or return-path event set.
- When a thread is stuck with an agent or a return is lost.

## Inputs
- Thread ID and current owner.
- Allowed actions and scope for this handoff.
- Sync engine lease API and TTL policy.

## Steps
1. Human initiates handoff in-thread; client sends `thread_id` plus a manifest (see `manifest.md`).
2. Sync engine mints a lease (`lease_id`, `ttl_seconds`, `single_writer_token`) and records the manifest.
3. Agent confirms `started` keyed by `(thread_id, lease_id)`; it may act only within scope.
4. Agent emits `draft-ready` with revision hash, then `sent` after approval, or `failed` with reason.
5. On completion or TTL expiry, sync engine emits `returned` and restores human ownership.
6. Reject any agent event whose `lease_id` or single-writer token is stale.
7. Log every event to the audit trail.

## Output format
- The manifest object (from `manifest.md`).
- The ordered return-path event list with payload fields.
- Lease expiry and stale-token handling rules.

## Guardrails
- Key everything by `thread_id`; never copy the thread.
- One active lease per thread; single-writer token enforced.
- TTL is mandatory; no infinite leases.
- Agent acts only within manifest scope and allowed actions.

## Example
Manifest: `{thread_id: t_123, owner: agent, scope: reply, lease_id: l_9, ttl_seconds: 900, allowed_actions: [draft_reply]}`. Agent emits `started`, then `draft-ready` (hash h1). After approval, `sent`. Sync engine emits `returned`. See `manifest.md`.

# Frozen Envelope & Approval

## Overview
The agent receives a frozen thread envelope (participants, ordered message-ID set with watermark, attachments, labels, stated intent) and may only produce draft revisions inside it. Nothing sends until a human approves a specific revision hash. Handoff is a thread-local, time-boxed capability grant, and ownership state is rendered in the thread header and logged to an append-only audit trail.

## When to use
- When implementing the approval gate or the envelope the agent drafts within.
- When adding ownership state to the thread header or audit logging.
- When a send happened without approval or the agent acted outside scope.

## Inputs
- Thread participants, ordered message-ID set, attachments, labels.
- Human's stated intent for the thread.
- Grant scopes and TTL.

## Steps
1. Human initiates handoff; mint a signed, thread-local, time-boxed capability grant (thread ID, grantor, scopes, TTL).
2. Freeze the envelope: participants, ordered message-ID set with watermark, attachments, labels, intent. Hash it.
3. Agent drafts only inside the envelope; each revision gets a content hash.
4. Render owner state in the header: `human-owned`, `agent-proposed`, `agent-acting`, `agent-blocked-needs-human`, `returned`.
5. Human approves a specific revision hash; approval binds to that hash and the envelope hash.
6. Send only the approved revision; if the envelope changed, require re-approval.
7. Log every transition and action to the append-only audit trail with rationale.

## Output format
- The envelope object (from `checklist.md`).
- The grant record (scopes, TTL, grantor).
- Header state list and audit event fields.

## Guardrails
- Draft-only by default; no send without approval of a specific revision hash.
- Envelope change invalidates prior approval.
- Grant is thread-local and time-boxed, not account-wide.
- Every transition is visible in the header and logged.

## Example
Envelope hash e1, revision hash r1. Header shows `agent-proposed`. Human approves r1; send allowed. If a new message arrives (watermark moves), envelope hash changes and re-approval is required. See `checklist.md`.

kit_files.harness:
## Purpose This document specifies a harness design for an agent that can take over an email thread on behalf of a human, built for the product surface described publicly by Orchid (orchid.ai, formerly Zero and Mail0). The harness exists to answer one question safely: **how does a thread move from human-owned to agent-held and back without dropping the conversation?** The design treats handoff as a first-class, versioned, auditable state transition rather than a background action. It is organized around five artifacts, in priority order: 1. A versioned **Thread Handoff Contract** with a CAS-guarded state machine. 2. A **lease-return-path** owned by the sync engine, keyed by thread ID. 3. **Frozen-envelope approval** bound to a revision hash, draft-only by default. 4. A thread-local, time-boxed **capability grant** with a mandatory send gate. 5. **Visible ownership state** in the thread header plus an append-only audit trail. All numbers below are labeled **targets**, not results. No customer names, metrics, or quotes are claimed beyond what is publicly visible; where public information is thin, the design states its assumptions. ## Architecture The harness sits between the mail client, the sync engine, and one or more agents. The agent never holds a divergent copy of the conversation. - Every state transition is CAS-guarded on a monotonically increasing `state_version`; a stale writer loses. - The lease is owned by the sync engine, not the agent. Lease expiry returns the thread to the human automatically. - Nothing leaves draft state without a human approval bound to a specific revision hash. ## Agents and roles | Role | Type | Responsibility | May write | Must escalate when | |---|---|---|---|---| | Eligibility scorer | AI agent | Scores thread for agent-fit; proposes handoff | Score record only | Score below threshold | | Handoff confirmer | Human | Confirms or overrides eligibility; signs first-contact per account | Grant record | First contact on a new account | | Packet assembler | AI agent | Builds handoff packet: summary, intent, open questions, constraints, tone, deadlines, do-not-say list | Packet (immutable once sealed) | Intent ambiguous | | Permission checker | Hybrid | Verifies send-as identity, recipient scope, approval level | Check result | Identity or scope mismatch | | Thread agent | AI agent | Replies in-thread inside envelope; preserves quoting and subject | Draft revisions only | Low confidence, new intent, envelope breach | | Approver | Human | Approves a specific revision hash or rejects | Approval record | — (is the gate) | | Auditor / reclaimer | Human | Reviews audit trail; one-click reclaim | Reclaim event | Any anomaly | | Eval miner | AI agent | Mines handoffs for failures; proposes schema/prompt/escalation updates | Delta to anti-pattern list | — | Separation of duties: the thread agent can never approve its own revision, and the eligibility scorer can never mint a grant. ## Tools and MCP servers - **Mail MCP server** — `read_thread(thread_id, watermark)`, `create_draft(thread_id, revision)`, `send_draft(thread_id, revision_hash, grant_id)`, `apply_label`, `propose_archive`. Send is rejected unless the revision hash matches an approval record and the grant is unexpired. - **Calendar MCP server** — read-only deadline lookup for packet assembly. - **Knowledge MCP server** — tone guides, per-account do-not-say lists, prior packet schemas. - **Eval store** — offline fixtures and online trace sink; append-only. - **Audit log** — append-only, hash-chained; every tool call and transition lands here before its effect is visible. All tool calls carry `(thread_id, lease_id, state_version)`; the MCP layer enforces the single-writer token so a reclaimed thread's stale agent cannot write. ## Skills Three skills are mandatory and versioned alongside the contract: - **thread-handoff-contract** — Encodes the state machine (`unassigned -> offered -> agent-held -> awaiting-approval -> returned | reclaimed | failed`), the CAS rules, and the contract schema version. Any agent or service that touches thread state loads this skill first; it refuses transitions that skip the approval gate or reuse a stale `state_version`. - **lease-return-path** — Implements lease acquisition, TTL renewal, and the return-path event vocabulary (`started`, `draft-ready`, `sent`, `failed`, `returned`) keyed by `(thread_id, lease_id)`. Guarantees that lease expiry emits `returned` and flips ownership back to the human even if the agent dies silently. - **frozen-envelope-approval** — Builds the frozen envelope (participants, ordered message-ID set with watermark, attachments, labels, stated intent), hashes it, and binds approvals to draft revision hashes inside it. Rejects any draft that references messages beyond the watermark or alters quoting. ## State schema Single versioned record per thread, stored by the sync engine: ```json { "schema_version": "thc/1", "thread_id": "immutable", "state_version": 0, "state": "unassigned | offered | agent-held | awaiting-approval | returned | reclaimed | failed", "owner": {"type": "human | agent | none", "id": "..."}, "grant": {"grant_id": "...", "grantor": "...", "scopes": ["read_thread","draft_reply","apply_label","propose_archive"], "expires_at": "..."}, "lease": {"lease_id": "...", "ttl_s": 0, "renewed_at": "...", "single_writer_token": "..."}, "envelope": {"envelope_hash": "...", "watermark_message_id": "...", "participants": [], "attachment_hashes": [], "labels": [], "stated_intent": "..."}, "approval": {"revision_hash": "...", "approver": "...", "approved_at": "..."}, "events": [{"seq": 0, "type": "...", "actor": "...", "content_hash": "...", "at": "..."}] } ``` Rules: `thread_id` immutable; `events` append-only with content hashes; `state_version` increments on every transition and is the CAS guard; `approval.revision_hash` must match the draft being sent; a lease without a live grant is invalid. ## Workflow 1. **Eligibility gate (hybrid).** Scorer proposes; human confirms or overrides. No state change without confirmation. 2. **Handoff packet (agent).** Packet assembler seals an immutable packet inside the envelope. 3. **Permission and identity check (hybrid).** Verify send-as identity and recipient scope; human signs off on first contact per account. 4. **Grant and lease.** Client mints the thread-local grant; sync engine issues the lease with TTL and single-writer token; state moves `offered -> agent-held` via CAS. 5. **Agent acts.** Thread agent drafts revisions inside the envelope, preserving quoting and subject; emits `started` and `draft-ready`. 6. **Approval gate.** Human approves a revision hash; state moves to `awaiting-approval -> sent`; `send_draft` verifies hash and grant. 7. **Return or reclaim.** On completion, failure, or TTL expiry, the lease-return-path emits `returned` and ownership flips to the human; a human can reclaim at any time with one click. 8. **Audit and eval.** Every transition is logged with rationale; the eval miner diffs draft vs sent and writes one delta to the anti-pattern list. ## Guardrails and anti-patterns Guardrails: - Draft-only by default; send requires a hash-bound human approval and a live grant. - Single writer per thread enforced by lease token; stale writes rejected on `state_version`. - Envelope freeze: no new participants, attachments, or messages beyond the watermark without re-freezing and re-approval. - TTL expiry always returns the thread; no silent agent persistence. - Ownership state rendered in the thread header at all times; no background takeovers. - One-click human reclaim preempts the agent immediately. Anti-patterns the harness must refuse: - Handing over a **copy** of the thread instead of the ID. - Account-wide agent tokens instead of per-thread grants. - Approval bound to "the draft" rather than a revision hash. - Agents that can extend their own lease indefinitely. - Hidden ownership changes with no header state. - Sending on low confidence without escalation. - Audit entries written after the effect instead of before. ## Evals **Offline** (fixtures replayed against the harness): - CAS race: two writers, one stale — stale write must fail. Pass: 100% rejection of stale `state_version`. - Lease expiry mid-draft: `returned` emitted, ownership flipped, no orphan draft sent. Pass: 100%. - Envelope breach: draft referencing post-watermark message rejected. Pass: 100%. - Approval mismatch: send with wrong revision hash rejected. Pass: 100%. - Reclaim during send: human wins, agent notified. Pass: 100%. - Packet quality rubric (intent, constraints, do-not-say present). Pass target: ≥ 90% of fixtures score full marks. **Online** (production traces, sampled): - Handoff completion without drop: thread returns to human with conversation intact. Target: ≥ 99%. - Approval-gate integrity: zero sends without matching approval record. Target: 100%. - Escalation precision on low confidence / new intent. Target: ≥ 95% recall on labeled traces. - Time-to-reclaim under one click. Target: p95 < 2 s. - Audit completeness: every transition has a pre-effect log entry. Target: 100%. ## QHX improvement loop Every production run writes exactly **one delta** to the anti-pattern list — a single, specific, testable addition (e.g., "agent renewed lease past grant expiry," "packet omitted do-not-say on forwarded threads"). The eval miner drafts the delta, a human ratifies it, and the next offline fixture set includes a regression case for it. The anti-pattern list is versioned with the contract; a delta that recurs twice triggers a schema or skill revision, not just a prompt tweak. ## Rollout plan **Days 0–30.** Ship the Thread Handoff Contract v1 and CAS state machine behind a flag; internal threads only. Build the audit log and header ownership state. Offline evals green on CAS, expiry, and approval mismatch. **Days 31–60.** Enable lease-return-path and frozen-envelope-approval for a small internal cohort; draft-only, human approves every send. Start the QHX loop; ratify the first anti-pattern deltas. Target: zero approval-gate violations. **Days 61–90.** Open handoff to external recipients on opted-in accounts with first-contact human sign-off; enable one-click reclaim and online eval sampling. Review contract at v1.x with deltas folded in.
